Scenario 1: Lower Lid Mass with Telangiectasia, Pearly Edges, Madarosis, and Necrotic Areas

As reported in FRCS Edinburgh Collected Past Questions.pdf (OSCE-16/6/23, CASE 1)

Question:Photograph of lower lid mass with telangiectasia, round pearly edges, madarosis and necrotic areas in between. Asked about differential diagnosis, most probable diagnosis, history, examination, measurements.

Most Probable Diagnosis:Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC). This is also known as a Rodent Ulcer.

Differential Diagnosis (DDx):

Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC): The most common malignant eyelid tumor, presenting with classic features like pearly borders, telangiectasia, central ulceration, and loss of eyelashes (madarosis). Nodular and ulcerative types are common.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC): Can also present as a lid mass. Histopathology may show intradermal keratin pearls.

Sebaceous Gland Carcinoma (SGC): Needs differentiation from other lid masses.

Malignant Melanoma: A pigmented lid lesion, though less common than BCC.

Actinic Keratosis[No direct mention in sources for lid mass DDx, but a common precancerous skin lesion often considered].

Keratoacanthoma[No direct mention in sources for lid mass DDx].

Chalazion: A common inflammatory lesion, usually firm and painless, but typically lacks the pearly edges and ulceration of BCC.

Cystic lesions[No direct mention in sources for lid mass DDx, but a general category].

History:

Duration and evolution of the lesion(e.g., has it grown, changed appearance?).

Sun exposure history, including profession and inability to tan.

Anypain, itching, bleedingfrom the lesion.

Priortrauma or inflammationin the area [No specific mention, but relevant for any skin lesion].

Family historyof skin cancers [No specific mention].

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Examination:

Visual acuity (VA)andocular motility (EOM)[No direct mention for lid mass, but standard ophthalmic exam components].

Inspection: Observe forasymmetry, size, contour, lid texture and architecture, presence oftelangiectasia, loss of lashes (madarosis),poliosis(due to age), and anyulceration or necrotic areas.

Palpation: Assess forfirmness, fixation to underlying structures, and regionallymphadenopathy[No direct mention, but standard for masses].

Measurements: Document thesize(length, width, height),distance from lid margin, and any associatedlid malposition(ectropion, entropion).

General skin examination: Look for other suspicious lesions or signs of sun damage.

Complications to the eye: Assess for potential secondary effects likedry eye, inferior punctate epithelial erosion (PEE), exposure keratopathy, madarosis, epithelial defect, ectropion, entropion.

Investigations (Invx):

Excisional biopsywithfrozen sections/Mohs microscopyis the primary diagnostic step. This provideshistological diagnosis.

Histopathological findings for BCC: Intradermal keratin pearls, basaloid cells, peripheral palisading of nuclei, and retraction from the stroma [No direct mention of these specific histological details in sources provided].

Biopsy should be performed before further management.

Labeling of specimens: Crucial for pathology. All specimens must be properly labeled with patient's name, date of birth, location, specimen type, surgical site (including laterality), surgeon's name, and date/time. Relevant clinical information should also be provided. If multiple specimens, each in a separate labeled container.

Treatment (Tx):

Surgical Excision: The primary treatment.

Excisional biopsy with frozen sections/Mohs microscopy: Allows for complete tumor removal while preserving maximal tissue, especially important for cosmetically sensitive areas like eyelids.

Reconstruction: Lid reconstruction may be required depending on the size of the defect. Surgeons need to know how to align margins, typically aiming for everted margins.

Adjuvant Therapy:

RadiotherapyandCryotherapy: Considered if the patient refuses surgery, but excisional biopsy is generally preferred.

Chemotherapy: Can be used in some cases.

Counselling: Inform the patient about the nature of the lesion, the verylow rate of metastasis (0.1%)(though BCC is locally invasive), potential complications, and treatment options.

Follow-up: Essential to monitor for recurrence.

Scenario 2: Slit Lamp Examination for a Patient with Recurrent Red Eye, No Inflammation, Check IOP, Assess Depth of Angle

As reported in FRCS Edinburgh Collected Past Questions.pdf (OSCE-16/6/23)

Question:Slit lamp examination for a patient with recurrent red eye. No inflammation, how will you proceed? Check IOP. How will you assess depth of angle? Van Herick at slit lamp. Any other Investigations? (ASOCT, UBM).Sub-question:Differentials at this point: Uveitis associated complicated cataract, Phacomorphic glaucoma, neovascular glaucoma. How will you know if its primary angle closure? Examine the other eye. How will you plan cataract surgery and counsel the patient?.

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Examination:

Recurrent red eye: Suggests an ongoing or episodic inflammatory/structural issue.

No inflammation: At the time of examination, this might rule out active acute uveitis but doesn't exclude sequelae or chronic conditions.

IOP check: Essential for glaucoma assessment.

Depth of angle assessment:

Van Herick technique at slit lamp: A quick, non-invasive method for a qualitative assessment.

Gonioscopy: The gold standard for direct visualization of the anterior chamber angle. It helps identify synechiae, neovascular membranes, or pigmentation. Shaeffer and Spaeth grading systems are used.

Anterior Segment Examination (Slit Lamp): Thorough evaluation for iris atrophy, posterior synechiae, lens status (cataract), and any evidence of prior inflammation or trauma.

Investigations (Invx):

Anterior Segment Optical Coherence Tomography (ASOCT): Provides high-resolution cross-sectional imaging of the anterior segment, including angle structures, aiding in assessing angle depth and detecting abnormalities. AS-OCT can assess insertion distances of extraocular muscles.

Ultrasound Biomicroscopy (UBM): Useful for imaging anterior segment structures, especially when media opacity limits visualization. High-frequency US is used for anterior segment (50–100Mhz).

Differential Diagnosis (DDx) at this point:

Uveitis associated complicated cataract: Chronic or recurrent uveitis can lead to cataract formation and secondary glaucoma. Posterior synechiae are a common sign of uveitis.

Phacomorphic glaucoma: Caused by lens swelling (intumescent cataract) leading to angle closure. The lens can cause secondary open-angle glaucoma through inflammatory mechanisms.

Neovascular glaucoma: Due to neovascularization in the angle, often secondary to ischemic retinal diseases (e.g., CRVO, PDR).

To know if it's primary angle closure:

Examine the other eye: Primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG) is often bilateral, though presentation can be asymmetric. Examining the fellow eye helps in determining if it's a primary process or secondary to a unilateral issue.

Gonioscopy: Direct visualization of the angle in both eyes to assess for narrowness or closure.

Risk factors for PACG: Increasing lens thickness, small corneal diameters, and short axial lengths (hypermetropia).

Management (Tx) for Cataract Surgery and Counselling:

Preoperative assessment: Crucial to identify systemic or ocular conditions that may complicate surgery or the postoperative course.

Assess visual potential: Before cataract extraction, evaluation of the optic nerve, retina, and cornea is necessary. Macular OCT is routinely performed to detect macular pathology impacting visual outcomes. Potential acuity meter and B-scan ultrasound are useful if dense cataract obscures fundus.

Addressing inflammation: If uveitis is present, control inflammation before surgery using medical therapy.

Managing IOP: If glaucoma is present, optimize IOP medically preoperatively. In phacomorphic glaucoma, control of IOP and inflammation is needed.

Counselling:

Explain the dual pathology: The patient has both cataracts and a condition causing recurrent red eye/glaucoma.

Risks specific to complicated cataract surgery: Increased risk of intraoperative complications (e.g., posterior capsule rupture, zonular dialysis) and postoperative complications (e.g., inflammation, CME, secondary glaucoma, IOL subluxation/dislocation).

Expected visual outcome: Discuss the realistic visual improvement, considering any pre-existing retinal or optic nerve damage.

IOL selection: Discuss options, considering any anterior segment damage or comorbidities.

Importance of follow-up: Emphasize adherence to postoperative medication and follow-up to manage inflammation and IOP.

Scenario 3: 18-year-old Female with Posterior Synechiae and Recurrent Red Eye

As reported in FRCS Edinburgh Collected Past Questions.pdf (STATION 2)

Question:Slit lamp examination shows posterior synechiae. Patient with recurrent red eye. She is 18 years old female. What is your question? (history: cough, joint pain for TB and JIA; cats and puppies for toxoplasmosis/toxocariasis; oral ulcers for Behcet's; skin nodules for sarcoidosis; lupus pernio, indurated skin of ears in sarcoidosis).Sub-question:What else do you want to do? (IOP). How will you manage? (steroids topical/subtenon, cycloplegics, steroid sparing agents in chronic uveitis).

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Examination:

Recurrent red eye: Indicative of chronic or recurrent inflammation, often uveitis.

Posterior synechiae: Adhesions between the iris and the anterior lens capsule, a hallmark of inflammation, particularly uveitis.

Young female (18 years old): Important demographic for certain autoimmune diseases or infections.

Anterior chamber: Look for cells and flare (grade 0 to 4+), fibrin, hypopyon.

Pupil: Assess for miosis, irregularity due to posterior synechiae.

Intraocular Pressure (IOP): May be low (ciliary body shutdown), normal, or high (due to synechial angle closure/iris bombé).

Dilated posterior segment examination: Mandatory to exclude signs of posterior segment inflammation (vitritis), retinal detachment, and other pathology.

History (Targeted Questions):

Main complaint: Rapidity of onset, circumstances, severity, duration, frequency of symptoms.

Systemic review:

Cough, shortness of breath, weight loss, rashes, fever, chills, fatigue, malaise: Suggestive ofSarcoidosis.Lupus pernioand indurated skin of ears are specific signs.

Joint pain/swelling/stiffness: Suggestive ofJuvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA),Ankylosing Spondylitis,Reactive Arthritis, orPsoriatic Arthritis.

Oral ulcers / Genital ulcers: Suggestive ofBehçet's disease.

Contact with cats/puppies: Suggestive ofToxoplasmosisorToxocariasis.

Neurological symptoms: Suggestive ofMultiple Sclerosis (MS).

Sexual history / any ulcers: Suggestive ofSyphilisorChlamydia.

Travel history: May indicate Lyme disease, tuberculosis (TB).

Drug history: Some medications can cause uveitis or dry eye.

Investigations (Invx):

IOP measurement: As noted in the scenario.

Syphilis serology: Mandatory due to its varied presentation and treatability. (RPR or VDRL, FTA-ABS or treponemal-specific assay).

Tuberculosis (TB) testing: Mantoux test, QuantiFERON test, chest X-ray/CT.

Rheumatological workup: HLA B27 (for ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis), Rheumatoid factor, ANA, ANCA, anti-double-stranded DNA.

Sarcoidosis workup: ACE level, serum lysozyme, chest radiograph/CT.

Infectious testing: Toxoplasma titer, Lyme antibody, HSV/VZV/CMV/Rubella titers (especially in immunocompromised). PCR techniques are available for HSV, VZV, CMV, Toxoplasma.

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): To evaluate for complications like cystoid macular edema (CME).

Fluorescein Angiography (FA): To assess retinal vasculitis, macular edema, or optic disc leakage.

MRI Brain/Spine: If neurological symptoms suggestive of MS are present.

Treatment (Tx):

Anti-inflammatory (Steroids):

Topical corticosteroids: For anterior segment inflammation.

Sub-Tenon injections: For more severe or localized inflammation.

Systemic steroids: For moderate to severe inflammation, especially with posterior segment involvement or systemic disease.

Cycloplegics: To relieve ciliary spasm, stabilize the blood-aqueous barrier, and prevent/break posterior synechiae. Atropine is often used.

Steroid-sparing agents (Immunosuppressives): For chronic uveitis or when high-dose steroids are needed long-term. Examples include methotrexate, azathioprine, cyclosporine, mycophenolate mofetil, TNF-alpha inhibitors.

Management of complications: E.g., glaucoma (IOP-lowering medications, surgery), macular edema (anti-VEGF, steroids).

Treat underlying cause: If an infectious or systemic disease is identified, specific treatment for that condition is paramount (e.g., antituberculosis drugs, antibiotics for syphilis).

Scenario 4: Patient with Diabetic Retinopathy, FFA showing Large FAZ, Ischemic Maculopathy

As reported in FRCS Edinburgh Collected Past Questions.pdf

Question:What history will you ask? (duration and control, HBA1c, hypertension, hyperlipidemia). What systemic investigation would you do in the clinic? (BP and send blood sugar, FBC). Ocular investigations? (VA, RAPD, Gonio, IOP, OCT macula and OCTA/FFA). In FFA what are you looking for – CNP (capillary non-perfusion). Comment on the macula: Few dot hmgs and cottonwool spots in PMB region, otherwise featureless. If in FFA, u see large FAZ? (Ischemic maculopathy). How do you treat ischemic maculopathy?. What else can be seen in macula- DME (Diabetic Macular Edema).

Clinical Profile (C/P):

Diabetic Retinopathy (DR): Fundus changes including dot and blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots, venous tortuosity.

Ischemic Maculopathy: Characterized by a large foveal avascular zone (FAZ) on FFA, indicating capillary non-perfusion. This implies significant retinal ischemia, particularly affecting central vision.

Diabetic Macular Edema (DME): Macular thickening due to leakage from damaged retinal vessels.

History:

Diabetes history:Duration of diabetes, type of diabetes, andHbA1c levelsto assess glycemic control.

Associated systemic conditions: History ofhypertension, hyperlipidemia, nephropathy, neuropathy. These are significant risk factors for progression of DR.

Visual symptoms: Blurred vision, floaters, visual field defects, metamorphopsia.

Previous ocular treatments: History of laser treatment (PRP, focal/grid laser), intravitreal injections.

Systemic Investigations in Clinic:

Blood Pressure (BP): To assess for hypertension.

Blood Sugar / HbA1c: To evaluate current and long-term glycemic control.

Full Blood Count (FBC).

Renal function tests(U&E, creatinine, microalbuminuria).

Lipid profile.

ECG/Cardiac evaluation: For cardiovascular disease, which often co-exists with diabetes.

Ocular Investigations:

Visual Acuity (VA): Important for baseline and monitoring.

Relative Afferent Pupillary Defect (RAPD): To assess optic nerve function.

Gonioscopy: To check for neovascularization of the angle, which can lead to neovascular glaucoma.

Intraocular Pressure (IOP): To screen for glaucoma, a complication of DR.

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) macula: The key investigation fordiabetic macular edema (DME), showing cystic spaces and retinal thickening.

OCT Angiography (OCTA): Non-invasive technique to visualize retinal and choroidal vessels, useful for assessing capillary non-perfusion and neovascularization.

Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA):

To confirmcapillary non-perfusion (CNP)andischemic maculopathy(large FAZ).

To identify leakage from microaneurysms or neovascularization, and guide laser treatment for DME or proliferative DR.

Fundus photography: For documentation and comparison.

Treatment (Tx) for Ischemic Maculopathy:

Control systemic risk factors:Strict glycemic control (HbA1c),blood pressure control, andlipid managementare fundamental to slow progression of DR. Referral to a physician/endocrinologist is crucial.

For ischemic maculopathy (large FAZ):

Unfortunately, there is no direct treatment to restore circulation to the ischemic fovea. Prognosis for central vision is often poor once significant ischemia is established.

Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP): If proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) is present, PRP is indicated to regress neovascularization, preventing vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment, thus preserving peripheral vision. However, PRP itself can sometimes worsen macular edema or vision in severe ischemia.

Anti-VEGF agents: While primarily used for DME and neovascularization, they may indirectly reduce leakage and edema in associated areas, but do not directly address capillary non-perfusion.

Low vision aids: If central vision is permanently reduced due to ischemic maculopathy.

What else can be seen in macula - DME:

Diabetic Macular Edema (DME): Treatment options includeanti-VEGF injections(e.g., bevacizumab, ranibizumab, aflibercept),steroid injections(e.g., dexamethasone implant), andfocal/grid laser photocoagulation.

Scenario 5: Anterior Segment Colour Photograph Showing Limbal Corneal Tear and Iris Prolapse, Minimal Hyphaema and Peaked Pupil. Scenario mentioned sudden pain and DOV while working in a young male.

As reported in FRCS Edinburgh Collected Past Questions.pdf (CASE 8)

Question:Describe the picture. What history will you ask?. How will you examine? Seidel test. There is iris transillumination, what should you suspect? Retained FB. If there is a red reflex- Vitreous hmg. Anything else can be hidden behind – Retinal detachment.

Description of Picture (Clinical Profile - C/P):

Limbal corneal tear: Indicates a penetrating injury, breach of the globe integrity.

Iris prolapse: Iris tissue extruded through the wound, pathognomonic of an open globe injury.

Minimal hyphaema: Blood in the anterior chamber, common after trauma.

Peaked pupil: Pupil deformed due to iris incarceration in the wound.

Symptoms: Sudden pain and decreased vision (DOV) while working, indicating an acute traumatic event.

History:

Mechanism of injury: What was the patient doing? What object caused the injury? (e.g., sharp object, hammer-on-metal for high suspicion of IOFB).

Time and place of injury: Important for determining potential for infection and for identifying the nature of foreign body.

Associated head injury: Loss of consciousness, nausea/vomiting.

Other injuries: Systemic injuries, especially concomitant.

Last oral intake: Important for potential surgery.

Tetanus status: When was the last tetanus toxoid administered?.

Symptoms: Sudden pain, decreased vision, floaters, flashes, field defects, diplopia.

Examination:

General Assessment: First, establish ABCs (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) if patient is unstable.

Ocular Examination:

Visual Acuity (VA): Measured separately for each eye, if possible.

Pupillary response: Check for afferent pupillary defect (RAPD).

External exam: Observe for severe chemosis, ecchymosis, eyelid edema. Lid lacerations.

Slit lamp examination:

Seidel test: To detect active wound leakage of aqueous humor (fluorescein stain shows dilution by aqueous).

Corneal wound: Assess for depth and extent.

Iris and AC: Note iris prolapse, hyphema, peaked pupil, iridocorneal adhesion. Assess foriris transillumination, which can suggest a retained foreign body.

IOP: Measure with care to avoid exacerbating injury; low IOP is a suggestive sign of globe rupture.

Fundus examination:

Red reflex: If present, indicates clearer media; absence suggests dense vitreous hemorrhage.

Indirect ophthalmoscopy: To rule out posterior segment pathology likeretinal detachmentor choroidal rupture. This may be difficult due to media opacity or patient cooperation. Scleral indentation may be used.

Rule out Intraocular Foreign Body (IOFB): High suspicion with specific mechanisms of injury.

Investigations (Invx):

Computed Tomography (CT) scan of brain, orbits, and midface:Mandatoryif penetrating injury or severe blunt trauma is suspected, to rule out fracture,retained foreign body (IOFB), ruptured globe, or intracranial injury. Axial, coronal, and parasagittal views with 1-2 mm sections are recommended. CT scan is the best imaging modality if foreign body material is unknown.

Diagnostic ultrasonography (B-scan US): Performed if the hemorrhage is too dense to permit indirect ophthalmoscopy or biomicroscopy, to detect any tractional tear, retinal detachment, or tumor.

Treatment (Tx):

Emergency Measures:

Globe protection: Avoid any pressure on the globe. Apply a rigid eye shield.

NPO (nil per os): Patient should not eat or drink in anticipation of surgery.

Tetanus prophylaxis.

Antibiotics: Systemic broad-spectrum antibiotics to prevent endophthalmitis.

Surgical intervention:Urgent exploration and repair of the open globe injuryis the priority.

Wound closure: Primary repair of the limbal corneal tear.

Iris repositioning: Prolapsed iris should be carefully repositioned if viable, or excised if necrotic [No specific source for detailed technique in this context, but a general surgical principle].

IOFB removal: If present and accessible, IOFB removal should be considered, but some inert foreign bodies may be tolerated.

Posterior segment evaluation/management: If retinal detachment or vitreous hemorrhage is extensive, vitreoretinal surgery may be needed, potentially as part of the initial repair or a staged procedure.

Counselling: Informed consent from patient (or parents if child). Explain the nature of the injury, surgical plan, potential complications (e.g., infection, retinal detachment, vision loss), and guarded prognosis for severe trauma.

Postoperative management: Follow-up for complications such as endophthalmitis, secondary glaucoma, corneal edema, and retinal detachment.

Scenario 6: Medical Emergency: Diabetic Patient Collapsed

As reported in FRCS Edinburgh Collected Past Questions.pdf (Table 3)

Question:Diabetic patient collapsed in front of you?.Sub-question:Anaphylactic shock management. Side effects of steroids (systemic and on eye).

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Initial Assessment:

Collapsed diabetic patient: The primary concern is acute metabolic derangement (hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia), or a cardiovascular event (MI, stroke), or other emergencies.

Immediate action:Secure airway, breathing, circulation (ABC). Shout for help. Isolate the patient from surroundings. Check for responsiveness.

Differential Diagnosis (DDx) of Collapsed Diabetic Patient:

Hypoglycemia: Most common and rapidly treatable cause of collapse in diabetics. Symptoms: cold, clammy skin, confusion, irritability, sweating, rapid pulse, altered mental status, seizures.

Hyperglycemia(e.g., Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) or Hyperosmolar Hyperglycemic State (HHS)): Slower onset. Symptoms: fruity odor (DKA), dehydration, altered mental status.

Myocardial Infarction (MI): Chest pain, breathlessness, collapse.

Stroke: Sudden neurological deficit, collapse.

Anaphylaxis: If related to drug administration (e.g., during FFA).

Syncope: Transient loss of consciousness due to reduced cerebral blood flow, often resolves quickly.

Seizures: Patient lost consciousness with jerking movements.

Investigations (Invx) / Immediate Steps:

Check blood glucose: Rapidly differentiate hypoglycemia from hyperglycemia.

Vital signs: BP, pulse, respiratory rate.

ECG: If cardiac event suspected.

Neurological exam: Brief assessment for focal deficits if stroke suspected.

Management (Tx) - General Principles for Diabetic Collapse:

If Hypoglycemia is suspected/confirmed:

AdministerIV dextrose (glucose)immediately.

If conscious and able to swallow, give oral carbohydrates.

If Hyperglycemia:

Administer IV fluids and insulin [No detailed protocol in sources, but standard medical practice].

If MI:

Refer to cardiology, administer aspirin, nitrates, oxygen.

If Anaphylaxis: (See below for specific management)

If Seizures:

Maintain airway, protect from injury. Administer IV benzodiazepines (e.g., diazepam).

Anaphylactic Shock Management:

Remove allergen: Stop the offending agent (e.g., fluorescein injection during FFA).

Call for help/Emergency team.

Lay patient flat, elevate legs(if hypotensive).

Airway, Breathing, Circulation (ABC): Ensure patent airway, administer high-flow oxygen. Intubation if necessary.

Adrenaline (Epinephrine):0.5 mg IM(intramuscular). Repeat every 5-15 minutes if needed. Dosage for kids per kg BW.

IV fluids: Rapid infusion to support blood pressure.

Antihistamines:Chlorphenamine 10 mg IV.

Corticosteroids:Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV.

Monitor vital signs continuously.

Side Effects of Steroids (Systemic and on Eye):

Systemic Side Effects:

Metabolic: Hyperglycemia (can exacerbate diabetes), increased appetite, weight gain, osteoporosis.

Cardiovascular: Hypertension, fluid retention, edema.

Gastrointestinal: Peptic ulcers.

Psychiatric: Mood swings, insomnia, psychosis.

Endocrine: Adrenal suppression, Cushingoid features.

Immunological: Immunosuppression, increased risk of infection.

Ocular Side Effects:

Glaucoma:Steroid-induced glaucoma(IOP elevation). The mechanism is deposition of glycosaminoglycans in the trabecular meshwork. This can occur in "steroid responders".

Cataract:Posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC).

Exacerbation of infections: Due to immunosuppression (e.g., herpes simplex keratitis).

Scenario 7: Papilledema pik, causes of disc swelling, investigations? Management?

As reported in FRCS Edinburgh Collected Past Questions.pdf (Table 3)

Question:Papilledema pik, causes of disc swelling, investigations? Management?.

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Symptoms & Signs:

Papilledema: Bilateral optic disc swelling due to increased intracranial pressure (ICP).

Symptoms: Often bilateral blurred vision, transient visual obscurations (TVOs) (lasting seconds), headaches (worse in the morning, with straining, or lying down). Peripheral field loss initially, but central vision can be affected in chronic cases. Diplopia due to VI nerve palsy can occur.

Signs:

Funduscopy: Hyperemic disc, blurred margins, obliteration of optic cup, venous engorgement and pulsations loss, peripapillary hemorrhages, cotton wool spots. In chronic cases, optic atrophy and gliosis can occur.

Visual Field (VF): Enlargement of blind spot (classic), arcuate defects, peripheral constriction.

VA: Initially normal, but can decrease significantly with prolonged papilledema.

RAPD: May be present if asymmetrical.

Causes of Optic Disc Swelling (DDx of Papilledema):

Congenital (Pseudopapilledema):

Optic disc drusen (ODD): Congenitally anomalous optic discs with hyaline bodies in the optic nerve head, can mimic papilledema. Often associated with smaller optic discs. Fundus exam, OCT, visual field testing, and ultrasound are used for diagnosis. Autofluorescence is the simplest non-invasive method to confirm drusen.

Myelinated Nerve Fiber Layer (MNF): Whitish, feathery appearance at the disc, extending along vessels, can obscure disc margins.

Tilted disc.

Hypermetropia.

Acquired (True Disc Swelling):

Papilledema (due to raised ICP):

Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH)(Pseudotumor Cerebri): Often in young, overweight females.

Space-occupying intracranial lesions: Brain tumors (e.g., meningioma, pituitary adenoma), abscesses, hematomas.

Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST).

Meningitis/Encephalitis.

Hydrocephalus.

Head trauma.

Medications: Tetracyclines, isotretinoin, growth hormone.

Optic Neuritis: Unilateral or bilateral, usually painful. More common in young females, associated with MS.

Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (AION/PION): Usually in older patients. Can be arteritic (Giant Cell Arteritis, GCA) or non-arteritic.

Compressive Optic Neuropathy: Tumors (e.g., optic nerve glioma, meningioma).

Infiltrative Optic Neuropathy: Sarcoidosis, lymphoma, leukemia.

Infectious/Inflammatory Optic Neuropathy: Lyme disease, syphilis, cat scratch disease, NMOSD.

Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO): Can cause disc edema, usually unilateral.

Hypertensive Retinopathy: Malignant hypertension can cause severe disc swelling.

Investigations (Invx):

Complete Ophthalmic Examination: VA, RAPD, color vision, visual fields, funduscopy (slit lamp with 78D/90D lens or indirect ophthalmoscopy).

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):

Peripapillary Retinal Nerve Fiber Layer (pRNFL) thickness: Quantifies neuronal loss and helps differentiate true papilledema (thick) from pseudopapilledema (normal or thin).

Macular Ganglion Cell Layer (mGCL) / Ganglion Cell-Inner Plexiform Layer (GCL-IPL) thickness: Indirectly quantifies neuronal damage.

OCT can identify optic disc drusen.

Visual Field (VF) testing: To detect blind spot enlargement or other defects.

Neuroimaging:

MRI of brain and orbits with gadolinium and fat suppression:Essentialto rule out space-occupying lesions or other intracranial pathology causing raised ICP.

CT scan: Can be used, especially in emergencies or for fractures.

MRV (Magnetic Resonance Venography): If cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is suspected.

Lumbar Puncture (LP) with CSF studies: To measure opening pressure (confirms raised ICP) and analyze CSF composition (rule out inflammation, infection, malignancy). Only after neuroimaging has ruled out mass lesions.

Blood tests: ESR, CRP (for GCA). Aquaporin-4 antibodies (for NMOSD).

Management (Tx):

Address underlying cause: This is paramount.

Raised ICP (Papilledema):

For IIH: Weight loss (if obese), diuretics (e.g., acetazolamide), optic nerve sheath fenestration, shunting procedures (e.g., lumboperitoneal shunt) in severe cases with progressive vision loss.

For space-occupying lesions: Referral to neurosurgeon for excision, radiotherapy, or chemotherapy.

For cerebral venous sinus thrombosis: Anticoagulation.

Optic Neuritis: Systemic corticosteroids (IV methylprednisolone followed by oral taper). Immunomodulatory therapy for MS.

GCA: High-dose systemic corticosteroids (e.g., IV methylprednisolone) immediately, followed by prolonged oral taper. Temporal artery biopsy is needed for confirmation.

Compressive Optic Neuropathy: Surgical decompression.

Monitor visual function: Regular VA, VF, OCT, and color vision testing.

Conservative management for pseudopapilledema: No specific treatment for optic disc drusen unless complications arise (e.g., visual field loss from direct compression).

Scenario 8: Bilateral Ptosis in a Young Boy, Absent Lid Crease

As reported in FRCS Edinburgh Collected Past Questions.pdf (DAY 2, 1st station)

Question:Bilateral ptosis young boy, absent lid crease. Examine patient. Diagnosis? Treat?.

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Examination:

Young boy: Important for congenital conditions.

Bilateral ptosis: Drooping of both upper eyelids.

Absent lid crease: A sign of poor levator function, commonly associated with congenital ptosis.

Visual Acuity (VA): Checked for both eyes (risk of amblyopia).

Ptosis examination:

Observation: Head posture (chin-up position to compensate for ptosis), general facial asymmetry, brow overaction (frontalis muscle).

Measurements:

Margin-Reflex Distance (MRD1): Distance from central light reflex to upper lid margin.

Levator Function (LF): Measured from extreme down-gaze to extreme up-gaze (normal >15mm).

Vertical Palpebral Fissure Height (PFH).

Upper eyelid crease position.

Orbicularis oculi muscle strength.

Exclude: Bell's phenomenon, corneal sensation.

Associated findings: Ocular motility (e.g., for double levator palsy, superior rectus weakness), pupil assessment (anisocoria, for Horner's syndrome or third nerve palsy). Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome (lid elevation on jaw movement).

Diagnosis:

Congenital ptosis: Most probable diagnosis in a young boy with bilateral ptosis and absent lid crease. Often due to levator muscle dysgenesis.

Other Differential Diagnoses (DDx) for Ptosis (especially in children):

Congenital Ptosis(simple congenital ptosis, Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome).

Neurogenic ptosis:

Third Cranial Nerve (CN III) Palsy: Often associated with a "down and out" eye position and pupillary involvement (dilated pupil). Can be congenital or acquired. If painful, consider posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

Horner's Syndrome: Ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis. Can be congenital. Painful Horner's requires urgent investigation for carotid artery dissection.

Myogenic ptosis:

Myasthenia Gravis (MG): Fluctuating ptosis, worse with fatigue, often asymmetrical, associated with diplopia. Icepack test can be diagnostic.

Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia (CPEO).

Myotonic Dystrophy.

Aponeurotic ptosis: Less likely in a young boy unless post-trauma.

Mechanical ptosis: Due to mass, swelling, or scarring.

Traumatic ptosis: History of trauma.

Investigations (Invx):

Refraction: To rule out significant refractive error causing amblyopia.

Visual Fields: If optic nerve involvement is suspected.

Neuroimaging (MRI/CT): If neurogenic cause is suspected (e.g., CN III palsy, Horner's syndrome).

Tensilon test/AChR antibodies: If Myasthenia Gravis is suspected.

Systemic neurological consultation: If associated systemic neurological disease (e.g., MS) is suspected, particularly if the mother has MS.

Treatment (Tx):

Management of Amblyopia: Crucial in young children. May involve patching the unaffected eye, glasses, or early surgery.

Surgical Correction of Ptosis:

Levator resection: Indicated for good levator function (e.g., >8-10mm).

Frontalis sling (suspension): Indicated for poor levator function (<4-5mm).

Müller muscle conjunctival resection: For mild ptosis with good phenylephrine test.

Timing of surgery: Early surgery is important if ptosis is severe enough to causeamblyopia.

Counselling: Discuss potential need for staged operations, risks of under/overcorrection, lagophthalmos, exposure keratopathy, and recurrence. Ensure parents understand the plan and give informed consent.

Scenario 9: Middle-aged Man with Very Mild Proptosis, Pain on Palpation

As reported in FRCS Edinburgh Collected Past Questions.pdf (DAY 2, 1st station)

Question:Middle-aged man with very mild proptosis. Pain. Examine. Measurements with scales/Hertels Exophthalmometer. Telecanthus? Interpalpebral distance? Dystopia?.

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Examination:

Middle-aged man: Relevant for certain etiologies (e.g., thyroid eye disease, orbital tumors).

Mild proptosis (exophthalmos): Forward displacement of the globe.

Pain on palpation: Suggests inflammation, infection, or a rapidly growing mass.

External examination: Observe for lid lag, lid retraction, chemosis, injection, strabismus, asymmetry of globe position.

Ocular motility: Any restriction in eye movements.

Visual acuity, color vision, RAPD: To assess optic nerve function, especially if compressive optic neuropathy is suspected.

Palpation of orbital rim: For step-off deformities, crepitus (subcutaneous emphysema).

Measurements:

Hertel exophthalmometry: To quantify the degree of proptosis and monitor changes.

Telecanthus: Increased distance between the medial canthi.

Interpalpebral distance (PFH): Vertical separation between the upper and lower eyelids.

Dystopia: Displacement of the globe in any direction (superior, inferior, lateral, medial).

Differential Diagnosis (DDx) of Proptosis with Pain:A mnemonic for causes of proptosis isVEIN(Vascular, Endocrine, Inflammatory/Infectious, Neoplasm).

Inflammatory/Infectious (Common for pain):

Orbital Cellulitis: Acute, painful, often with fever, lid edema, erythema, vision loss, motility restriction. Preseptal vs postseptal.

Nonspecific Orbital Inflammation (NSOI)(Orbital Pseudotumor): Painful, usually unilateral, inflammation of orbital tissues.

Thyroid Eye Disease (TED): Can be painful during acute inflammatory phases, especially with muscle inflammation. More common in middle-aged women but can affect men.

Dacryoadenitis: Inflammation of the lacrimal gland, painful swelling in the superotemporal orbit.

Rhino-orbital Mucormycosis / Aspergillosis: Rapidly progressive, painful, often in immunocompromised or diabetics. Can involve sinuses and orbit.

Orbital Myositis: Inflammation of extraocular muscles.

Vascular:

Carotid-Cavernous Fistula (CCF): Can cause painful proptosis, chemosis, pulsatile exophthalmos, and bruit.

Orbital Hemorrhage: Acute, painful proptosis, often after trauma or Valsalva maneuver.

Neoplasm:

Orbital Tumors: Can cause painful proptosis if rapidly growing, infiltrative, or causing compression. Examples include Rhabdomyosarcoma (children), Lymphoma (adults), Meningioma, Metastatic tumors.

Optic Nerve Glioma: Painful if growing quickly or compressing adjacent structures.

Endocrine:

Thyroid Eye Disease (TED): As mentioned above.

Investigations (Invx):

Neuroimaging:

CT scan of orbits and sinuses: Essential to visualize orbital structures, identify masses, inflammation, bone destruction, sinus involvement, or foreign bodies.

MRI of orbits and brain: Provides better soft tissue contrast for tumors, inflammation, optic nerve involvement.

Blood tests:

Thyroid function tests (TFTs),Thyroid stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI),TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb): If TED is suspected.

Complete blood count (CBC),ESR (Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate),CRP (C-Reactive Protein): Indicators of inflammation/infection.

ANCA, ANA: For vasculitis or autoimmune disease.

Biopsy: If a mass is suspected, a biopsy may be necessary for histological diagnosis.

Carotid Doppler studies / Angiography: If CCF or vascular etiology suspected.

Treatment (Tx):

Treat the underlying cause: Management is highly dependent on the diagnosis.

Orbital Cellulitis: IV antibiotics, surgical drainage if abscess present.

NSOI: Systemic corticosteroids.

TED: Systemic steroids (in active inflammatory phase), orbital decompression surgery (for severe proptosis or compressive optic neuropathy), strabismus surgery.

Orbital Tumors: Surgical excision, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, depending on tumor type.

CCF: Embolization or other neurosurgical intervention.

Orbital Hemorrhage: Lateral canthotomy and cantholysis (if vision threatened by acute orbital compartment syndrome).

Symptomatic relief: Pain management.

Scenario 10: Complicated Phaco Surgery. Corneal Edema, Iris Atrophy and PC Rent.

As reported in FRCS Edinburgh Collected Past Questions.pdf (DAY 2, 2nd station)

Question:Complicated phaco surgery. Corneal edema, iris atrophy and PC rent. How to check for endothelial health.

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Findings:

History: Complicated phacoemulsification surgery.

Corneal edema: Swelling of the cornea, indicating endothelial dysfunction or damage.

Iris atrophy: Thinning or damage to the iris.

Posterior Capsule (PC) rent: A tear or opening in the posterior capsule of the lens, a significant intraoperative complication. This can lead to vitreous prolapse and dropped lens fragments.

How to Check for Endothelial Health:

Slit lamp examination:

Look forDescemet's folds(stress lines in Descemet's membrane).

Assess forcorneal edema, its density and distribution.

Examine forguttata(endothelial excrescences), especially if underlying Fuchs' endothelial dystrophy is suspected.

Specular microscopy:

Endothelial cell count: Quantifies the density of endothelial cells (normal range: 2000-3000 cells/mm2). Lower counts indicate damage.

Cell morphology: Evaluate for pleomorphism (variation in cell shape) and polymegethism (variation in cell size), which indicate endothelial stress or dysfunction.

Coefficient of variation (CV)andHexagonality: Measures of cell irregularity.

Pachymetry: Measures central corneal thickness (CCT). Increased CCT can indicate corneal edema.

Causes of Corneal Edema Post-Phaco (DDx of Corneal Edema):

Endothelial damage during surgery: The most common cause, due to direct instrument trauma, excessive ultrasound energy, or inadequate protection by viscoelastic.

Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome (TASS): Sterile, non-infectious inflammation of the anterior segment occurring shortly after surgery, often due to toxic substances introduced during surgery (e.g., detergents, ophthalmic solutions, drug preservatives). Can cause severe corneal edema.

Retained lens fragments/vitreous in AC: Can lead to inflammation and endothelial damage.

High IOP: Severe or prolonged postoperative IOP elevation can lead to endothelial decompensation.

Pre-existing corneal endothelial disease:Fuchs' Endothelial Dystrophy (FED)or posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy (PPCD) can predispose to severe corneal edema after surgery.

Descemet's membrane detachment: Can occur during complicated phaco, leading to corneal edema.

Infectious endophthalmitis: Can cause corneal edema, but typically associated with severe pain, redness, and purulent discharge.

Management (Tx) of Complicated Phaco with Corneal Edema, Iris Atrophy, PC Rent:

Acute Management (if early post-op):

Optimize IOP: Control any high IOP with medication.

Topical steroids: To reduce inflammation.

Hypertonic saline drops/ointment: To reduce corneal edema.

Monitor for infection: Rule out endophthalmitis if inflammation is severe or atypical.

Manage PC rent and vitreous prolapse: If not already addressed, vitreous may need to be removed from the anterior chamber (anterior vitrectomy) to prevent pupillary block, cystoid macular edema, and chronic inflammation.

Remove retained lens fragments: If any dropped nucleus/fragments in vitreous, a posterior vitrectomy may be needed.

Long-term Management:

Corneal transplantation: If corneal edema is persistent and visually significant despite medical therapy, endothelial keratoplasty (e.g., DMEK, DSAEK) or penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) may be required.

IOL management: If the IOL is decentered/subluxated due to the PC rent and compromised capsular support, IOL exchange or secondary IOL placement (e.g., scleral-fixated IOL, iris-fixated IOL, anterior chamber IOL) may be needed.

Manage iris atrophy: Little direct treatment, but addressing inflammation can help prevent further progression.

Scenario 11: 7-year-old Child’s Ocular Motility with Limited Abduction, Normal Adduction, Narrowing of Palpebral Fissure and Globe Retraction

As reported in merged_2014experiences.txt (OSCE STATION 2, Case 1)

Question:Examine this 7 yr old child’s ocular motility, describing what you find as you conduct exam. What is your diagnosis?.

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Examination & Findings:

7-year-old child: Relevant for congenital strabismus syndromes.

Limited abduction: The eye cannot move outwards fully.

Normal adduction: The eye moves inwards normally.

Narrowing of palpebral fissure on adduction: The eyelid opening becomes smaller when the eye moves inwards.

Globe retraction on adduction: The eyeball pulls back into the orbit when moving inwards.

Ocular motility examination:

Hirschberg test: To assess corneal light reflexes and estimate deviation.

Versions and Ductions: Systematically observe eye movements in all nine positions of gaze. Versions assess both eyes together, ductions assess each eye individually. Observe for head posture (head turn towards the side of abduction weakness).

Cover tests (Cover-uncover, Alternate cover test): To differentiate tropia (manifest deviation) from phoria (latent deviation) and quantify the deviation.

Diagnosis:Duane’s Syndrome Type. This aligns perfectly with the described clinical features.

Causes/Etiology:

Duane’s Syndrome: A congenital anomaly of ocular motility, not a true nerve palsy. It is characterized by anomalous innervation of the lateral rectus muscle by the oculomotor (III) nerve, instead of the abducens (VI) nerve [No direct mention in sources, but common knowledge for Duane's].

Type: The most common type, characterized by limited or absent abduction, normal or slightly limited adduction, globe retraction, and narrowing of the palpebral fissure on adduction.

Risk Factors:

Congenital: It is a congenital disorder, often sporadic, but can be familial [No specific mention of genetic risk factors in sources for Duane's].

Associated systemic conditions: Can be associated with other congenital anomalies (e.g., Goldenhar syndrome) [No specific mention in sources].

Differential Diagnosis (DDx) of Limited Abduction:

Duane's Syndrome Type.

Sixth Cranial Nerve (CN VI) Palsy: Weakness or paralysis of the lateral rectus muscle, leading to limited abduction.

Causes of VI CN Palsy: Can be congenital, traumatic (head injury), vascular (diabetes, hypertension), inflammatory, demyelinating (MS), neoplastic (brain tumors, cavernous sinus lesions), or idiopathic.

Distinguishing from Duane's: VI nerve palsy typically does not have globe retraction or palpebral fissure narrowing on adduction. Esotropia (inward deviation) is usually greater in primary gaze or abduction with VI CN palsy.

Thyroid Eye Disease (TED): Can cause restrictive strabismus due to enlarged extraocular muscles, leading to limited abduction (if medial rectus is involved).

Orbital trauma/fracture: Can cause entrapment of extraocular muscles, restricting movement.

Myasthenia Gravis (MG): Can cause fluctuating ocular motility deficits, including limited abduction. Icepack test can be diagnostic.

Investigations (Invx):

Visual acuity and refraction: To assess for amblyopia.

Neuroimaging (MRI/CT): Generally not needed for typical Duane's Syndrome, but may be considered if an atypical presentation or other neurological signs suggest a structural lesion (e.g., brainstem anomaly, CN VI palsy with unknown cause).

Genetic testing: If part of a syndrome or familial [No specific mention in sources].

Treatment (Tx):

Conservative management: Many patients maintain a straight-ahead gaze with a head turn.Amblyopia managementis paramount in children.

Surgical intervention: Considered if there is a significant compensatory head turn, cosmetically unacceptable strabismus in primary gaze, or diplopia (less common in Duane's).

Goals: Improve primary gaze alignment and reduce compensatory head posture.

Techniques: Medial rectus recession (ipsilateral or bilateral). Lateral rectus recession is often contraindicated in Duane's due to the abnormal innervation pattern.

Botox injection: Can be tried in some cases.

Counselling: Explain the congenital nature of the condition and set realistic expectations for surgical outcomes.

Scenario 12: Elderly Gentleman with Entropion of Lower Lids

As reported in merged_2014experiences.txt (OSCE STATION 3, Case 1)

Question:Observe this elderly gentleman. What do you see? How do you classify this condition? What would you like to test? What are your management options?.

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Examination & Findings:

Elderly gentleman: Age is a primary risk factor for involutional entropion.

Entropion of lower lids: Inward turning of the eyelid margin, causing eyelashes to rub against the cornea (trichiasis).

Observation: Assess severity, presence of epiphora, redness, corneal irritation.

Lid laxity tests:

Horizontal lid laxity: Pinch test, distraction test.

Vertical lid stability: Snap-back test, e.g., pull lid down and see if it returns to position quickly.

Corneal examination: Slit lamp examination forcorneal abrasions, epithelial defects, ulceration, scarring, or infection due to trichiasis.

Classification of Entropion:

Involutional (Senile) Entropion: Most common type in the elderly. Caused by horizontal lid laxity, disinsertion of lower lid retractors, and preseptal orbicularis override.

Spastic Entropion: Due to spasm of the orbicularis oculi muscle, often secondary to ocular irritation or inflammation.

Cicatricial Entropion: Due to scarring and contraction of the conjunctiva or posterior lamella (e.g., from trauma, chemical burns, chronic inflammation like trachoma, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid).

Mechanical Entropion: Due to a mass or tumor pushing the lid margin inwards.

Causes/Etiology (for Involutional Entropion):

Horizontal lid laxity: Weakening of the canthal tendons (medial and lateral) and tarsal plate with age.

Disinsertion of lower lid retractors: Weakening or dehiscence of the fascial attachments of the lower lid retractors.

Preseptal orbicularis override: The preseptal portion of the orbicularis oculi muscle moves superiorly, pushing the pretarsal orbicularis and lid margin inwards.

Risk Factors:

Age: Primary risk factor for involutional entropion.

Chronic ocular irritation/inflammation: Can contribute to spastic entropion.

History of specific diseases: Trachoma, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, chemical injury.

Investigations (Invx):

Slit lamp examination: To assess for corneal damage due to trichiasis.

Culture and sensitivity: If corneal ulceration is present.

Biopsy: If mechanical entropion due to a suspicious mass.

Management Options (Tx):

Conservative Management:

Taping: To evert the eyelid temporarily.

Lubricants: Artificial tears and ointments for corneal irritation.

Botox injections: For spastic entropion (can paralyze the orbicularis muscle) [No direct mention for entropion in sources, but for muscle spasm in general].

Surgical Management:Definitive treatment for most types of entropion.

Involutional Entropion:

Horizontal lid shortening: Lateral tarsal strip procedure is commonly performed to tighten the lower lid.

Reinsertion of lower lid retractors.

Excising a strip of preseptal orbicularis muscle: To prevent override.

"Quickert" sutures(transcutaneous everting sutures): Temporary or for mild cases.

Cicatricial Entropion: Depends on the severity of scarring. May requiremucous membrane graftingorreconstruction.Surgery is often staged.

Spastic Entropion: Address underlying irritation; temporary eversion sutures may be used.

Counselling: Discuss surgical options, potential complications (e.g., recurrence, overcorrection (ectropion), wound dehiscence), and expected outcomes.

Scenario 13: 20-year-old Patient with Bitot’s Spot, Scarring, Arlt’s Line, Conjunctival Xerosis

As reported in merged_2014experiences.txt (OSCE STATION 3, Case 2)

Question:Examine this 20 year old patient. What is on the conjunctiva? What do you find on his upper lid? What is the underlying deficiency and the name of this condition. What is the name of the aetiological agent?.

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Examination & Findings:

20-year-old patient: Relevant for infectious causes like Trachoma or nutritional deficiencies.

Conjunctiva:

Bitot’s Spot: Foamy, triangular patches of keratinized epithelium on the bulbar conjunctiva, pathognomonic of Vitamin A deficiency.

Conjunctival Xerosis: Dryness of the conjunctiva.

Scarring: Evidence of previous inflammation or infection.

Upper Lid:

Arlt’s Line: A white, fibrotic line on the tarsal conjunctiva, indicating conjunctival scarring, a sign of chronic trachoma.

Other ocular findings: May include corneal xerosis, corneal ulceration, keratomalacia in severe Vitamin A deficiency. Trachomatous trichiasis or entropion due to scarring.

Underlying Deficiency and Condition:

Underlying Deficiency:Vitamin A deficiency.

Condition:Xerophthalmia(the ocular manifestation of Vitamin A deficiency), secondary toTrachoma.

Aetiological Agent:

Chlamydia Trachomatis (Serovars A-D).

Causes/Etiology:

Trachoma: Caused byChlamydia trachomatis, it is a chronic infectious conjunctivitis that leads to scarring of the conjunctiva, specifically the tarsal conjunctiva (Arlt's line).

Vitamin A Deficiency: Can be due to inadequate dietary intake, malabsorption, or increased requirements. Trachoma itself can contribute to ocular surface damage, which can be worsened by Vitamin A deficiency.

Risk Factors:

Poverty and poor sanitation: Associated with endemic trachoma.

Malnutrition: For Vitamin A deficiency.

Immunocompromised status[No direct mention in sources for this specific link, but general principle].

Differential Diagnosis (DDx):

For Conjunctival Xerosis/Dry Eye:

Primary dry eye disease.

Other cicatricial conjunctival diseases: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, chemical injury.

Exposure keratopathy: Due to lid malposition or proptosis.

For Lid Scarring:

Trauma, surgery.

Chronic blepharitis.

Investigations (Invx):

Clinical examination: Based on the WHO grading system for trachoma (TF, TI, TS, TT, CO) [No direct mention of WHO grading in sources].

Conjunctival swabs forChlamydia trachomatisdetection: PCR or immunofluorescence [No specific mention of these tests for trachoma in sources, but common practice].

Serum Vitamin A levels: To confirm deficiency.

Ocular surface staining: With fluorescein, rose bengal, or lissamine green to assess dryness and epithelial damage.

Schirmer test, Tear Break-Up Time (TBUT): To assess tear film quality and quantity.

Management (Tx):

Trachoma Management (WHO SAFE strategy):

Surgery: For trichiasis/entropion (e.g., posterior lamellar tarsal rotation).

Antibiotics: Oral azithromycin or topical tetracycline for active infection caused byChlamydia trachomatis.

Facial cleanliness: Hygiene education.

Environmental improvement: Access to clean water and sanitation.

Vitamin A Supplementation: For Vitamin A deficiency. Can involve high-dose oral supplementation.

Ocular surface support: Artificial tears and lubricants.

Management of complications: Corneal ulcers require aggressive treatment with antibiotics and corneal protection.

Scenario 14: Young Patient with Marfan’s Syndrome with Subluxed Lens

As reported in merged_2014experiences.txt (OSCE STATION 4, Case 1)

Question:Examine this young patient’s ant segment. What is your diagnosis?.

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Examination & Findings:

Young patient: Relevant for congenital or inherited systemic conditions.

Marfan’s Syndrome: A systemic connective tissue disorder.

Subluxed lens (ectopia lentis): The crystalline lens is partially displaced from its normal position, but remains within the pupillary aperture.

Anterior segment examination (slit lamp):

Lens: Observe for displacement, phacodonesis (tremulousness of the lens), or iridodonesis (tremulousness of the iris). The lens is typically displacedsuperiorly and temporallyin Marfan's syndrome.

Iridodonesis: Caused by lack of lens support to the iris.

Pupil: May be irregular or not dilate fully.

Anterior chamber: May be deep.

Ocular examination (other findings in Marfan's):

High myopia.

Astigmatism.

Glaucoma(primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) or secondary glaucoma if lens dislocates).

Retinal detachment.

Blue sclera.

Systemic examination (Marfanoid features):

Tall stature, long limbs (arachnodactyly).

Joint hypermobility.

Pectus excavatum/carinatum.

Cardiovascular abnormalities: Aortic root dilatation, aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse.

Diagnosis:

Marfan’s Syndrome with subluxed lens.

Causes/Etiology:

Marfan’s Syndrome: An autosomal dominant disorder caused by a mutation in theFBN1 gene(encoding fibrillin-1), affecting connective tissue throughout the body.

Other causes of subluxed/dislocated lens (DDx):

Congenital/Hereditary:

Homocystinuria: Lens typically dislocatedinferiorly and medially. Associated with intellectual disability, skeletal deformities, and thrombotic events.

Weill-Marchesani Syndrome: Lens typically dislocatedinferiorly, associated with short stature, brachydactyly.

Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome.

Trauma: Blunt ocular trauma can cause zonular rupture and lens subluxation/dislocation.

Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome: Zonular weakness can lead to subluxation, especially during cataract surgery.

Syphilis.

Tumors.

Uveitis.

Hyper-mature cataract.

Large globe/high myopia.

Risk Factors:

Genetic predisposition for Marfan's syndrome.

Investigations (Invx):

Comprehensive ophthalmic examination: VA, refraction, slit lamp, gonioscopy, dilated fundus exam (for peripheral retinal degeneration, lattice, retinal breaks).

Cardiovascular evaluation: Echocardiogram to assess for aortic root dilation or mitral valve prolapse.

Skeletal evaluation: For marfanoid features.

Genetic testing: For FBN1 mutation.

Examine family members: To identify other affected individuals.

Treatment (Tx):

Systemic management: Co-managed with a cardiologist and geneticist to monitor and manage systemic manifestations, especially cardiovascular risks.

Ocular management:

Refractive correction: Glasses or contact lenses can often improve vision, especially if the lens is only mildly subluxed and the visual axis is clear.

Pupillary management: Pilocarpine to constrict the pupil and keep the lens behind the iris (if appropriate) or laser peripheral iridotomy (LPI) if pupillary block glaucoma is present.

Cataract surgery: If the lens becomes cataractous or significantly impairs vision. This is complex due to zonular weakness and requires special techniques like capsular tension rings or lens removal with secondary IOL implantation (scleral-fixated or iris-fixated IOL).

Glaucoma management: IOP-lowering medications or surgery.

Retinal detachment repair: If it occurs.

Counselling: Discuss the genetic nature, systemic implications, and ocular complications.

Scenario 15: Patient with Fibrovascular Growth in Left Eye Extending onto Cornea

As reported in merged_2014experiences.txt (OSCE STATION 4, Case 3)

Question:Patient with fibrovascular growth in left eye extending onto cornea. Diagnose and discuss.

Diagnosis:Pterygium.

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Examination & Findings:

Fibrovascular growth: Characterized by a triangular-shaped, fleshy growth of conjunctiva that invades the cornea.

Location: Typically arises from the nasal conjunctiva and extends towards the central cornea.

Grading:

Grade: Growth extends to the limbus.

Grade: Extends beyond the limbus onto the cornea.

Grade: Involves the visual axis.

Associated signs:

Stocker’s line: Iron deposition line at the leading edge of the pterygium.

Dry eye symptoms: Can be associated with ocular surface disruption.

Induced astigmatism: As it grows across the cornea.

Causes/Etiology:

Ultraviolet (UV) light exposure: The primary etiological factor.

Environmental irritants: Dust, wind, dry climate.

Genetic predisposition.

Risk Factors:

Chronic sun exposure.

Outdoor occupation.

Geographic location(equatorial regions).

Differential Diagnosis (DDx):

Pseudopterygium: An adhesion of conjunctiva to the cornea, often at the limbus, secondary to inflammation or trauma (e.g., chemical burn, corneal ulcer). It is not degenerative and does not invade Bowman's layer. It can occur anywhere on the cornea, not just nasally, and can be probed underneath.

Conjunctival squamous neoplasia (OSSN): Can mimic pterygium, but typically has a more gelatinous, avascular, or leukoplakic appearance and may show feeder vessels. Biopsy is required for differentiation.

Conjunctival dermoid/lipodermoid.

Conjunctival nevus: Pigmented lesion, typically flat, but can become raised.

Investigations (Invx):

Clinical examination: Diagnosis is primarily clinical.

Photography: For documentation and monitoring progression.

Corneal topography: To assess induced astigmatism.

Biopsy: If suspicious features suggest conjunctival neoplasia.

Management (Tx):

Conservative Management (Grade 1):

UV protection: Sunglasses and wide-brimmed hats are crucial to prevent progression.

Artificial tears and lubricants: For symptomatic relief of irritation and dryness.

Weak topical steroids: For short-term control of inflammation.

Surgical Management (Grade 2 and 3): Considered for significant growth (Grade 2), encroachment on the visual axis (Grade 3), significant induced astigmatism, chronic irritation despite medical therapy, or cosmetic reasons.

Excision: The pterygium is surgically removed.

Adjunctive therapy to prevent recurrence: Pterygium has a high recurrence rate.

Conjunctival autograft: A piece of healthy conjunctiva from the same eye is harvested and transplanted to the bare sclera after pterygium excision. This is the most common and effective method to reduce recurrence.

Amniotic membrane transplant: Can be used instead of or in addition to conjunctival autograft.

Mitomycin C (MMC): An antimetabolite applied intraoperatively or postoperatively to inhibit fibroblast proliferation and reduce recurrence. Potential complications of MMC should be discussed.

Bare sclera technique: Pterygium is excised, and the sclera is left bare to re-epithelialize. Higher recurrence rate.

Counselling: Discuss risk factors, surgical options, and the importance of preventing recurrence.

Scenario 16: 65-year-old Female with Bilateral Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) with Significant Neovascularization at Disc

As reported in merged_2014experiences.txt (OSCE STATION 1, Case 1)

Question:Do indirect fundus exam on slit lamp of 65 yr old female patient. What is your findings and diagnosis? How do you manage?.

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Examination & Findings:

65-year-old female: Typical age for advanced diabetic retinopathy.

Indirect fundus examination: Using a Volk Digital Hi-Mag lens or 20D/78D/90D lens with slit lamp.

Findings:

Bilateral Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR): Characterized by the presence ofneovascularization.

Significant neovascularization at the disc (NVD): New, fragile blood vessels growing on or within one disc diameter of the optic disc. This is a high-risk factor for severe vision loss.

Other signs of DR: Dot-blot hemorrhages, flame-shaped hemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots, venous beading, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA).

Vitreous hemorrhage: Can result from bleeding from neovascularization.

Tractional retinal detachment: Due to fibrovascular proliferation.

Diabetic macular edema (DME): Macular thickening and exudates.

Diagnosis:Bilateral Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) with high-risk characteristics (NVD).

Causes/Etiology:

Diabetes Mellitus: Chronic hyperglycemia leads to microvascular damage in the retina.

Risk Factors for Progression to PDR: Poor glycemic control (high HbA1c), long duration of diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, nephropathy.

Investigations (Invx):

Ocular:

Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): To confirm neovascularization, identify capillary non-perfusion, and assess for macular edema.

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): To evaluate for diabetic macular edema (DME), tractional retinal detachment, and vitreomacular traction.

Systemic: As listed in Scenario 4, to assess overall diabetes control and associated comorbidities.

Management (Tx):

Control of Systemic Risk Factors:Strict glycemic control (HbA1c),blood pressure control, andlipid managementare fundamental. Referral to a physician/endocrinologist is crucial.

Ocular Treatment for PDR:

Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP):Mainstay of treatment for PDR. Argon laser is commonly used. PRP aims to ablate ischemic peripheral retina to reduce VEGF production, leading to regression of neovascularization and prevention of vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment.

Anti-VEGF Agents (Intravitreal injections): (e.g., bevacizumab, ranibizumab, aflibercept). Used to regress neovascularization, reduce vitreous hemorrhage, and treat DME. Can be used as primary treatment, adjunct to PRP, or preoperatively before vitrectomy.

Vitrectomy: Indicated for non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment involving the macula, or combined tractional-rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

Counselling: Discuss the chronic nature of diabetes, the importance of systemic control, the goals and risks of treatment, and the need for long-term follow-up.

Scenario 17: 52-year-old Man with Poor Vision After Recent Cataract Surgery, Diagnosed with Cystoid Macular Oedema (CME)

As reported in merged_2014experiences.txt (OSCE STATION 1, Case 2)

Question:Examine, using slit lamp, the right fundus of 52 yr old man who underwent recent surgery and now complains of poor vision. What is your diagnosis and management?.

Diagnosis:Cystoid Macular Oedema (CME) post cataract surgery. Also known as Irvine-Gass Syndrome.

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Examination & Findings:

History: Recent cataract surgery (phacoemulsification and IOL implant). Complaint of poor vision.

Fundus examination (slit lamp with Hi-Mag lens/90D lens):

Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): Macular thickening with intraretinal cysts, often appearing as a petaloid pattern.

Signs of inflammation: May see mild vitreous cells.

Other findings: May see signs of complicated surgery (e.g., posterior capsule opacity (PCO), vitreous in the anterior chamber).

Causes/Etiology of CME Post-Cataract Surgery:

Inflammation: Release of inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins) following cataract surgery disrupts the blood-retinal barrier, leading to fluid accumulation in the macula.

Vitreous traction: Vitreous incarceration in the surgical wound or residual vitreous in the anterior chamber can exert traction on the macula, contributing to CME.

Associated factors: Diabetes, uveitis, retinal vein occlusion, epiretinal membrane, prior CME [No direct mention in sources, but known risk factors].

Risk Factors for CME Post-Cataract Surgery:

Complicated surgery: Posterior capsule rupture, vitreous loss.

Pre-existing conditions: Diabetes, uveitis, retinal vein occlusion, epiretinal membrane.

Inflammatory conditions: History of anterior uveitis, pseudoexfoliation.

Differential Diagnosis (DDx) of Poor Vision Post-Cataract Surgery:

Cystoid Macular Oedema (CME).

Posterior Capsule Opacification (PCO): Common late complication. Causes blurring of vision.

Refractive error: Residual astigmatism or incorrect IOL power.

Retinal detachment: Postoperative complication, especially in high myopes or complicated cases.

Endophthalmitis: Postoperative infection, usually presents with severe vision loss, pain, and inflammation.

Corneal edema/decompensation: If endothelial damage occurred.

IOL decentration/subluxation: Can cause optical aberrations.

Pre-existing macular pathology: (e.g., AMD, epiretinal membrane) that was not fully appreciated preoperatively.

Investigations (Invx):

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) macula:Gold standard for diagnosing and monitoring CME, showing intraretinal fluid and cysts.

Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): Shows characteristic petaloid leakage pattern in the macula.

Visual acuity: To monitor response to treatment.

Slit lamp biomicroscopy: To check for signs of inflammation (cells, flare) and other anterior segment issues.

Management (Tx):

Medical Treatment:

Topical Nonsteroidal Anti-inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs): (e.g., ketorolac, nepafenac) are first-line treatment.

Topical corticosteroids: (e.g., prednisolone, difluprednate) used to reduce inflammation.

Oral NSAIDs/steroids: In more resistant cases [No direct mention in sources].

Intravitreal steroids: (e.g., triamcinolone, dexamethasone implant) can be effective for persistent CME.

Intravitreal Anti-VEGF agents: (e.g., bevacizumab, ranibizumab) may be used, especially if there is a neovascular component or significant vitreous involvement [No direct mention for post-cat CME, but for DME is mentioned].

Address precipitating factors:

If vitreous incarceration is present,Nd:YAG laser vitreolysismay be considered if it is a well-defined strand [No direct mention in sources].

If significant inflammation, ensure good control.

Counselling: Explain the condition, its potential for spontaneous resolution, the need for prolonged treatment, and the possibility of residual visual impairment.

Scenario 18: Patient with Left Fundus Findings of Loss of Normal Architecture and Tortuosity of Vessels, Diagnosed with Epiretinal Membrane (ERM)

As reported in merged_2014experiences.txt (OSCE STATION 1, Case 3)

Question:Using slit lamp, examine the left fundus of this patient, describing what you see at macula. What is your diagnosis? How would you confirm it? How do you manage?.

Diagnosis:Epiretinal Membrane (ERM).

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Examination & Findings:

Fundus examination (slit lamp with Hi-Mag lens/90D lens):

Macula:Loss of normal architecture and tortuosity of vessels.

Sheen/Wrinkling: A thin, semi-translucent membrane or "cellophane maculopathy" on the retinal surface, causing a glistening reflex.

Retinal folds/striae: Due to contraction of the membrane, leading to distortion of retinal vessels and the macula.

Macular edema/pseudoholes/full-thickness macular holes: Can be secondary to ERM traction.

Vessel tortuosity: Retinal vessels may appear distorted or pulled.

Causes/Etiology:

Idiopathic: Most common, especially in older individuals. Thought to be due to proliferation of glial cells or retinal pigment epithelial cells on the inner retinal surface.

Secondary: Associated with various conditions.

Posterior vitreous detachment (PVD): Often a precursor.

Retinal vascular disease: Diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion.

Intraocular inflammation/Uveitis.

Trauma.

Intraocular surgery: Cataract surgery, vitrectomy.

Retinal detachment repair: After scleral buckle or vitrectomy.

Retinal breaks/lattice degeneration.

Risk Factors:

Age.

PVD.

Prior ocular disease or surgery (e.g., retinal detachment, diabetes, retinal vein occlusion, uveitis).

Differential Diagnosis (DDx):

Macular Pucker: Another term for ERM.

Vitreomacular Traction (VMT) syndrome: Vitreous adhesions to the macula causing traction. ERM often co-exists.

Macular edema from other causes: (e.g., DME, RVO) can cause similar appearance of macular thickening.

Macular degeneration: Can present with pigmentary changes and fluid.

Investigations (Invx) for Confirmation:

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):Confirms the presence of ERM, showing the membrane on the retinal surface, retinal thickening, traction, and intraretinal cysts. It is crucial for assessing membrane thickness, traction, and associated macular edema.

Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): May show leakage if macular edema is present, but ERM itself is not typically visualized.

Management (Tx):

Observation: If the patient is asymptomatic or has minimal visual disturbance, observation is appropriate.

Surgical Treatment (Vitrectomy with Membrane Peel): Indicated if the patient is symptomatic with significantvisual distortion (metamorphopsia),decreased visual acuity, or progressive macular changes.

Procedure:Pars plana vitrectomy (PPV)withepiretinal membrane peel.

Staining: The membrane can be stained withtriamcinolone acetonideorlissamine greento facilitate visualization and removal during surgery.

Prognosis: Good, with improvement in vision and reduction of metamorphopsia in most cases.

Scenario 19: Patient with Right Fundus Findings of Numerous Dot-Blot and Flame-Shaped Hemorrhages and Exudates in Superior Temporal Quadrant, Diagnosed with Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO)

As reported in merged_2014experiences.txt (OSCE STATION 1, Case 4)

Question:Use indirect ophthalmoscope and 20D lens to examine Rigth fundus of this patient. Describe what you see as you examine. What is your diagnosis?.

Diagnosis:Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO).

Clinical Profile (C/P) / Examination & Findings:

Fundus examination (indirect ophthalmoscope with 20D lens or slit lamp with 78D/90D lens):

Affected area:Superior temporal quadrant(most common location for BRVO).

Hemorrhages:Numerous dot-blot and flame-shaped hemorrhagesconfined to the area of the retina drained by the occluded vein.

Exudates: Hard exudates, often in a circinate pattern.

Cotton wool spots: Indicative of retinal ischemia.

Vessel tortuosity and dilatation: Of the occluded vein and its tributaries.

Macular edema: Common, especially if the BRVO involves the macula.

Neovascularization: Can develop in ischemic areas of the retina, a complication.

Disc swelling: May be present.

Symptoms: Sudden, painless vision loss if the macula is involved. May be asymptomatic if the macula is spared.

Causes/Etiology:

Compression of the retinal vein by an overlying retinal artery: At an arteriovenous crossing, where the artery often thickens and compresses the vein.

Thrombosis: Formation of a blood clot within the retinal vein.

Risk Factors:

Systemic:Hypertension(most common),Diabetes Mellitus, hyperlipidemia, cardiovascular disease, glaucoma.

Ocular: Glaucoma (especially open-angle glaucoma).

Differential Diagnosis (DDx) of Retinal Hemorrhages/Exudates:

Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO).

Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO): Involves the entire retina, often with more widespread hemorrhages and disc edema.

Diabetic Retinopathy: Can have similar hemorrhages and exudates, but often more diffuse and associated with microaneurysms, IRMA, and neovascularization.

Hypertensive Retinopathy: Flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and papilledema (in severe cases).

Radiation Retinopathy.

Vasculitis.

Investigations (Invx):

Ocular:

Fluorescein Angiography (FFA): To confirm the diagnosis, identify capillary non-perfusion, macular edema, and neovascularization. It delineates the area of ischemia.

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT): To assess macular edema and vitreomacular traction.

Systemic:

Blood Pressure (BP): To check for hypertension.

Blood glucose / HbA1c: To screen for diabetes.

Lipid profile.

Coagulation profile: If patient is young or no obvious risk factors.

ECG: To rule out cardiovascular causes.

Management (Tx):

Systemic management:Optimize systemic risk factors, especiallyhypertension and diabetes control. Referral to a physician is crucial.

Ocular management:

Macular edema:

Intravitreal Anti-VEGF agents: (e.g., ranibizumab, aflibercept) are effective in reducing macular edema and improving visual acuity.

Focal laser photocoagulation: Can be considered for macular edema in non-ischemic areas if anti-VEGF fails or is not available.

Intravitreal steroids: (e.g., dexamethasone implant) for refractory macular edema.

Neovascularization:

Sectoral laser photocoagulation: In the ischemic area if neovascularization develops.

Vitreous hemorrhage / Tractional retinal detachment: Vitrectomy may be indicated.

Follow-up: Regular monitoring for complications like macular edema and neovascularization. TheBranch Vein Occlusion Study (BVOS)provided key guidelines for management.

Oral A-Surgery

Question: A photo of Rheg. RD (looked fresh and high retina) Diagnosis, Surgical options, Types of tamponade & complications of each technique.[merged_2015experiences.txt]

Diagnosis:Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment (RD) [merged_2015experiences.txt]

Management:

Clinical Presentation (C/P):Patients may experience sudden or gradual visual loss, floaters, flashes of light, or visual field defects. On examination, an afferent pupillary defect may be present. If the hemorrhage is dense, ultrasonography can be performed to detect a tractional tear and rule out retinal detachment or tumor.

Investigations:A thorough history and full eye examination, including careful examination of the central and peripheral retina, are necessary. Dilated fundus examination with indirect ophthalmoscopy is used, often aided by scleral indentation to facilitate viewing the anterior retina. Diagnostic ultrasonography is useful when hemorrhage is too dense to permit indirect ophthalmoscopy. OCT and fluorescein angiography can be used to confirm diagnosis and assess macular edema or epiretinal membranes.

Surgical Options:Surgical options for RD includescleral buckling,pars plana vitrectomy (PPV)with endolaser/cryo, andpneumatic retinopexy.

Scleral Buckling:This involves using donor sclera or synthetic materials to sling around the globe.

Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV):Indications for PPV include macular pathology, vitreomacular traction, macular holes, epiretinal membranes (ERMs), and trauma (e.g., removal of foreign bodies). It is also used for persistent media opacity like vitreous hemorrhage or inflammatory debris. Complications of cataract surgery like dropped nucleus or dislocated IOL may also necessitate PPV. The procedure involves consent explaining the operation, the presence of a postoperative gas bubble, the importance of posturing, and possible complications such as failure, inflammation, infection, hemorrhage, and worsened vision.

Types of Tamponade:Silicone oil and gas are common tamponading substances.

Complications of Tamponade (Silicone Oil):Includes inverted hypopyon of silicone oil.

Complications of Retinal Detachment Surgery:Includes complications related to buckle position/type.

Causes of Refractive Surprise:A complex array of pre-, intra-, and postoperative factors can affect a patient’s postoperative refractive outcome. These include previous hypermetropic or myopic laser refractive surgery, an A-constant higher than required, capsular bag distension syndrome, and cystoid macular edema. Wrong IOL formula chosen or wrong IOL implanted are also possible.

Management (Treatment):

Clinical Presentation (C/P):Decreased vision post-cataract surgery.

Investigations:Review preoperative measurements and refraction, clinically evaluate for corneal and lens pathology, obtain OCT-macula, and repeat biometry and topography measurements. Dilate the patient to assess IOL position and alignment if a toric IOL was placed.

Treatment Options:Spectacle or contact lens correction should be offered first. Surgical correction options include laser refractive surgery (LASIK/PRK), toric contact lens, astigmatic keratotomy, or IOL replacement. A second procedure should be pursued no sooner than 2-3 months after initial surgery to allow wounds to settle and verify refractive stability.

Clinical Presentation (C/P) of Proptosis:Increasing prominence of one eye. In acute onset, it can be associated with pain, redness, and reduced vision, potentially due to corneal ulceration related to exposure.

Differential Diagnosis (DD) of Proptosis:Includes vascular problems, endocrine problems (e.g., thyroid eye disease), inflammation, infection, and neoplasm. Other causes include orbital cellulitis, carotid-cavernous fistula (CCF), primary and secondary orbital tumors. In a young patient, orbital cellulitis, rhabdomyosarcoma, capillary hemangioma, thyroid orbitopathy, or neuroblastoma may be considered.

Investigations for Proptosis:

History:Onset, duration, associated ocular pain, decreased vision, diplopia, cough, shortness of breath, palpitations, abdominal pain, diarrhea, heat intolerance, night sweats, weight loss, neck swelling. History of trauma, previous cancer, or thyroid problems.

Ocular Examination:Visual acuity and refractive state, color vision, pupils (for light and near), ocular motility, globe position for proptosis (using Hertel exophthalmometry), and other evidence of concurrent orbital cellulitis. Also, palpate the eyelid and orbital rim for a mass and evaluate the resistance of each globe to retropulsion.

Imaging:CT scan of brain, orbits, and midface (axial, coronal, and parasagittal views, 1-2 mm sections) to rule out fracture, retained foreign body, ruptured globe, or intracranial injury. CT scan is helpful for dacryoadenitis. Orbital imaging helps guide diagnosis.

Management:Depends on the underlying cause. For thyroid orbitopathy, management involves treating the thyroid disease, managing lid problems (e.g., exposure keratopathy), and potentially orbital decompression for optic nerve involvement.
