Question: Obese lady with headache ….D.D. Benign increase intracranial tension….Tx ….weight loss advice …..same case If old lady and not obese.[merged_2015experiences.txt]

Condition:Benign Intracranial Hypertension (BIH), also known as Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension (IIH).

Clinical Presentation (C/P):Often seen in obese females, presenting with headaches and sometimes disc swelling. Vision may be good but visual fields may show enlargement of blind spots with a superotemporal defect. Optic nerve gliosis may also be present.

Differential Diagnosis (DD) for Disc Swelling:Includes pseudopapilledema, optic disc drusen, optic neuritis, ischemic optic neuropathy, compressive optic neuropathy, infiltrative optic neuropathy, traumatic optic neuropathy.

Investigations:

Ocular Examination:Fundoscopy for disc swelling. Visual field testing. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is helpful for differentiating papilledema from pseudopapilledema and identifying optic disc drusen and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness. OCT can also identify errors in segmentation due to disc edema.

Imaging:Magnetic Resonance Venography (MRV) to look at dural venous sinuses in obese patients. Brain imaging (MRI) in idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

Management:Treatment for BIH includes weight loss [merged_2015experiences.txt]. For severe cases with papilledema, referral to a neurosurgeon for potential space-occupying lesions.

Differential Diagnosis (DD) for Collapse:Hypoglycemia, syncope, cardiac arrest.

Prevention:Assess risk factors for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and minimize them (e.g., elastic stockings to prevent pooling of blood).

Examination Technique:Cover-uncover test.

Purpose:To detect heterotropias (cover component) and heterophorias (uncover component).

Procedure:

Cover Component:Cover the straight eye, look at the uncovered deviated eye; movement indicates tropia.

Uncover Component:Uncover the straight eye, look at the uncovered eye for deviation and refixation; movement indicates phoria.

Alternate Cover-Uncover Test:Detects heterophorias by alternating cover and uncovering both eyes and looking for movement in the uncovered eye.

Horizontal Motility Examination:Test extraocular movements (EOMs) in all nine positions of gaze. Evaluate versions (both eyes) and ductions (one eye). Reduced ocular motility should be assessed with a pen torch, paying careful attention to the position of corneal reflexes.

Condition:Angry eye with bullous keratopathy and rubeosis [merged_2015experiences.txt].

Rubeosis (Neovascular Glaucoma):New vessels seen at the pupil border.

Causes:Underlying disease is typically vascular, such as ischemic central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO), proliferative diabetic retinopathy, branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO), Eales disease, ocular ischemic syndrome, or trauma. Intraocular tumors or carotid cavernous fistula can also cause it.

Clinical Presentation (C/P):Ciliary injection, corneal clarity changes, microscopic hyphema in AC, AC depth changes. New vessels at the pupil border and iris.

Management:Difficult with usually very poor prognosis. Requires managing both the underlying disease and the neovascular glaucoma. If good visual potential, treatment involves panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) and intravitreal anti-VEGF injections. If poor visual potential and pain, cyclodestructive procedures or drainage devices may be considered.

Bullous Keratopathy:Cornea edema. Can be resolved with Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) or Descemet-stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK).

Management with Cataract:Two clinical problems managed simultaneously. Options include cataract extraction first with corneal transplantation (EK or PKP) later, or a triple procedure (combined cataract surgery and corneal graft).

Edrophonium Test (Tensilon Test):Diagnostic test for MG with 80% sensitivity.

Procedure:(Not fully detailed in sources, but implied to be a direct administration).

Side Effects:Hypotension, bradyarrhythmia, bronchospasm, SLUDGE (salivation/sweating, lacrimation, urination, defecation, giddiness, emesis).

False Positive:Eaton-Lambert syndrome, Guillain-Barre syndrome, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

Icepack Test:Another test for MG.

Management:Usually co-managed with a neurologist. Involves treating systemic condition and ocular complications.

1. DKA

Explanation of DKA (Diabetic Ketoacidosis):Not explicitly defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt," but indicated as a topic. DKA is a serious complication of diabetes that occurs when your body produces high levels of blood acids called ketones [Outside Source].

Causes & Risk Factors:Poorly controlled diabetes, especially Type 1, often triggered by infection, inadequate insulin, or stress [Outside Source].

Clinical Profile:Symptoms include polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, Kussmaul respirations, and a fruity odor on breath. Mental status can range from alertness to coma [Outside Source].

Investigations:Blood glucose levels (very high), urine ketones (positive), arterial blood gases (metabolic acidosis), electrolytes (potassium imbalances), complete blood count, and infection workup if suspected [Outside Source].

Management:Intravenous fluids, insulin therapy, electrolyte replacement (especially potassium), and treatment of underlying causes [Outside Source].

2. 35yr female with headache and dilated pupil (I gave DD of 3rd Nerve palsy due to aneurysm and Ophthalmoplegic Migraine)

Differential Diagnosis:

Third Nerve Palsy due to Aneurysm:This is a life-threatening cause. Aneurysms, particularly those of the posterior communicating artery, can compress the third cranial nerve, leading to ptosis, pupillary dilation, and impaired eye movements (adduction, elevation, depression). Pain is often a significant feature.

Ophthalmoplegic Migraine:A rare form of migraine characterized by recurrent attacks of headache associated with paresis of one or more ocular motor cranial nerves, typically the third nerve.

Adie's Tonic Pupil:Characterized by a unilaterally dilated pupil, often with light-near dissociation and vermiform movements of the iris on slit lamp exam. It is usually benign but can be associated with loss of deep tendon reflexes (Holmes-Adie Syndrome). Pharmacological testing with dilute pilocarpine (0.125%) can confirm the diagnosis by causing the affected pupil to constrict due to denervation supersensitivity.

Traumatic Mydriasis:Direct trauma to the iris can cause a dilated, irregular pupil.

Pharmacological Mydriasis:Accidental or intentional instillation of cycloplegic/mydriatic drops.

Investigations:

Urgent neuroimaging (MRI/MRA Brain) is crucial, especially to rule out an aneurysm. Consider CTA if MRI is not immediately available.

For isolated complete pupil-sparing 3rd nerve palsy (less likely with dilated pupil), imaging may not be immediately needed.

Pharmacological testing for Adie's pupil.

Management:

Manage the underlying cause (e.g., surgical clipping or coiling for aneurysm).

Address diplopia, if present, with prisms, patching, or surgery once the condition is stable.

3. Needle stick injury

Clinical Profile:History of accidental puncture by a needle or sharp instrument, potentially contaminated with blood or other bodily fluids.

Risk Factors:Healthcare workers, accidental punctures during medical procedures or handling contaminated waste [Outside Source].

Management:

Immediate First Aid:Encourage bleeding, wash thoroughly with soap and water, apply antiseptic [Outside Source].

Risk Assessment:Evaluate the source patient's infection status (HIV, Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C) and the nature of the injury (depth, visible blood) [Outside Source].

Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP):Administer appropriate PEP (antiretrovirals, Hepatitis B immunoglobulin/vaccine) based on risk assessment, typically within hours of exposure [Outside Source].

Follow-up:Serological testing for the exposed individual at baseline and at intervals (e.g., 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months) [Outside Source].

4. CMV retinitis atypical photo.(was more like frosted bite angitis)

Explanation of CMV Retinitis:Not explicitly defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt" beyond its mention. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis is an opportunistic viral infection of the retina, primarily seen in immunocompromised individuals, especially those with AIDS.

Clinical Profile (typical):Areas of retinal whitening and hemorrhage ("cottage cheese and ketchup" appearance), often with a brush-fire border of active infection. Visual symptoms include floaters, blurred vision, or visual field defects.

Clinical Profile (atypical/frosted bite angiitis-like):May present with sheathing of retinal vessels, appearing as "frosted branches" along the vasculature, which can be diffuse and resemble frosted bite angiitis.

Differential Diagnosis:

Frosted Bite Angiitis:A rare condition characterized by marked perivascular sheathing of retinal vessels, often idiopathic but can be associated with various systemic conditions or infections [Outside Source].

Progressive Outer Retinal Necrosis (PORN):Caused by varicella-zoster virus, seen in severe immunocompromise, characterized by rapid confluent outer retinal necrosis with minimal vitreous or anterior chamber inflammation.

Acute Retinal Necrosis (ARN):Caused by herpes simplex or varicella-zoster virus, typically occurs in immunocompetent individuals, characterized by peripheral retinal whitening, occlusive vasculitis, and prominent vitreous inflammation.

HIV Retinopathy:Microvascular changes (cotton wool spots, hemorrhages, microaneurysms) due to HIV itself, distinct from opportunistic infections.

Retinal Vasculitis:Can be due to various inflammatory or infectious causes.

Investigations:

Systemic Evaluation:HIV testing is crucial if not already known. CD4 count and viral load in known HIV patients [Outside Source].

Ocular Examination:Dilated fundus examination.

Anterior Chamber Paracentesis or Vitreous Tap:For PCR to identify the causative virus (CMV, HSV, VZV).

Management:

Antiviral Therapy:Systemic antivirals (e.g., ganciclovir, valganciclovir, foscarnet) are the mainstay of treatment [Outside Source].

HAART (Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy):For HIV patients, improving systemic immune status is key [Outside Source].

Monitoring:Regular ophthalmic follow-up for disease progression and potential complications like retinal detachment [Outside Source].

5. Ocular Lymphoma management

Clinical Profile:Ocular lymphoma can present in various forms, including intraocular lymphoma (vitreoretinal lymphoma), orbital lymphoma, or adnexal lymphoma.

Intraocular Lymphoma:May present with chronic, progressive vision loss, vitritis (vitreous cells and haze), subretinal infiltrative lesions, or retinal detachment. Often mimics chronic uveitis.

Orbital/Adnexal Lymphoma:Can cause proptosis, a palpable mass, lid swelling, or diplopia.

Differential Diagnosis:Uveitis (infectious/non-infectious), sarcoidosis, other inflammatory conditions, ocular metastases.

Investigations:

Ocular:

OCT:May show absence of cystoid macular edema and demonstrate subretinal infiltrative lesions.

Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA):May show blockage due to sub-RPE accumulation of lymphomatous cells ("leopard skin spots").

Ultrasound:May reveal vitreous debris, elevated subretinal lesions, retinal detachment, or thickening of the optic nerve.

Vitreous Biopsy/Tap:Cytology of vitreous samples or subretinal nodules is crucial for diagnosis. Immunohistochemistry based on cell-surface markers aids in classification.

Systemic:Systemic workup including neuroimaging (MRI brain), CSF analysis, and systemic biopsy (e.g., bone marrow, lymph node) to rule out systemic lymphoma [Outside Source].

Management:

Multidisciplinary Approach:Co-management with an oncologist is essential.

Treatment Options:Depends on the type and extent of lymphoma. Options include systemic chemotherapy, radiation therapy (external beam radiotherapy), or intravitreal chemotherapy [671, Outside Source].

6. TIA

Explanation of TIA:Transient Ischemic Attack. Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". A TIA is a temporary episode of neurological dysfunction caused by a brief interruption in blood supply to the brain or eye, without acute infarction.

Causes:Atherosclerosis (carotid artery stenosis, emboli from carotid arteries or heart), cardiac arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation), hypoperfusion, small vessel disease, hypercoagulable states.

Clinical Profile:Symptoms are transient and resolve completely, typically lasting less than 24 hours (often minutes). Ocular symptoms can include transient monocular visual loss (amaurosis fugax) or transient binocular visual loss (TBVL). Other neurological symptoms can include weakness, numbness, speech difficulties [Outside Source].

Risk Factors:Hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, smoking, atrial fibrillation, carotid artery disease, age.

Investigations:

History:Detailed history is key, including patient age, monocular/binocular vision loss, precipitating factors, pattern, duration, preceding/associated symptoms, and medical comorbidities.

Ocular Examination:Fundus examination for emboli (Hollenhorst plaques).

Cardiovascular Evaluation:ECG for arrhythmias (e.g., atrial fibrillation), echocardiogram for valvular heart disease or other cardiac sources of emboli.

Vascular Imaging:Carotid Doppler studies (ultrasonography) to rule out carotid stenosis, CT angiography (CTA) or MR angiography (MRA) of the head and neck.

Blood Tests:Complete blood count, lipid profile, fasting blood glucose, coagulation profile, and sometimes specific tests for hypercoagulable states (e.g., Protein S & C deficiency, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome).

Management:

Treat Underlying Cause:Manage hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia. Anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy for atrial fibrillation or other embolic sources.

Carotid Endarterectomy:May be indicated for significant carotid stenosis.

Lifestyle Modification:Smoking cessation, healthy diet, exercise [Outside Source].

II. Ophthalmic Medicine

1. Glaucoma drugs with classification. Advantage of timolol over PG analogue. Disadvantage of Alphagan

Classification of Glaucoma Drugs:

Prostaglandin Analogues (PGA):Latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost. Increase uveoscleral outflow.

Beta-blockers:Timolol, betaxolol. Decrease aqueous humor production.

Alpha-2 Adrenergic Agonists:Brimonidine (Alphagan), apraclonidine. Decrease aqueous humor production and increase uveoscleral outflow.

Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitors (CAI):Dorzolamide, brinzolamide (topical); acetazolamide (oral). Decrease aqueous humor production.

Rho Kinase Inhibitors:Netarsudil. Increase trabecular outflow.

Miotic Agents:Pilocarpine. Increase trabecular outflow.

Advantage of Timolol over PG Analogue:Not explicitly detailed in "merged_2016experiences.txt". PGAs are often first-line due to once-daily dosing and strong IOP lowering. However, timolol might be preferred in some cases if PGAs are contraindicated or not tolerated (e.g., side effects like iris pigmentation, eyelash growth, periocular skin darkening) [Outside Source]. Beta-blockers can also be less expensive.

Disadvantage of Alphagan (Brimonidine):Not explicitly detailed in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Common disadvantages include allergic conjunctivitis, follicular conjunctivitis, ocular dryness, fatigue, and drowsiness (especially in children, where it's contraindicated) [Outside Source].

2. Corneal ulcer with hypopyon. Same picture without corneal ulcer ie only hypopyon. Hypopyon in a patient with fever chills and sub ungual hemorrhages what is the diagnosis.(I could not answer--answer is infective endocarditis causing endogenous endoph)

Explanation of Hypopyon:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Hypopyon is a collection of white blood cells (pus) in the anterior chamber of the eye.

Corneal Ulcer with Hypopyon:

Causes:Bacterial (most common, e.g.,P. aeruginosa), fungal, amoebic (Acanthamoeba), or severe viral keratitis. Risk factors include contact lens wear (especially prolonged), trauma, ocular surface disease, immunosuppression.

Investigations:Corneal scraping for Gram stain, KOH prep, bacterial and fungal cultures. PCR for atypical cases.

Management:Intensive topical broad-spectrum antibiotics, antifungals, or anti-amoebic agents. Cycloplegics, systemic antibiotics in severe cases.

Hypopyon without Corneal Ulcer (Sterile Hypopyon):

Causes:Severe anterior uveitis (granulomatous or non-granulomatous, e.g., Behçet's disease, HLA-B27 associated), endophthalmitis (exogenous or endogenous), toxic anterior segment syndrome (TASS), masquerade syndromes (e.g., intraocular lymphoma).

Investigations:Thorough history and ocular examination. Aqueous tap for cell count, culture, PCR. B-scan ultrasound. Systemic workup if underlying systemic disease is suspected.

Hypopyon in patient with fever, chills, subungual hemorrhages:

Diagnosis:Infective endocarditis causing endogenous endophthalmitis. This is a severe systemic infection where bacteria from heart valves disseminate to the eye.

Clinical Profile (Endogenous Endophthalmitis):Hypopyon, vitritis, retinal infiltrates, fever, chills, new heart murmur, peripheral stigmata of endocarditis (Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions, Roth spots, subungual hemorrhages).

Investigations:Blood cultures (multiple sets), echocardiogram (transthoracic or transesophageal), vitreous tap for culture/PCR.

Management:Urgent systemic intravenous antibiotics, often for weeks. Intravitreal antibiotics may be needed. Vitrectomy if vision is poor or infection is severe.

Explanation of Infective Endocarditis:Not explicitly defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Infective endocarditis is an infection of the endocardium, the inner lining of the heart chambers and valves [Outside Source]. It is associated with ocular complications, including endogenous endophthalmitis.

3. CNVM with drusens

Explanation of CNVM:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Choroidal Neovascular Membrane, an abnormal growth of new blood vessels from the choroid into the subretinal space, often associated with Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD).

Explanation of Drusens:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Drusens are yellowish-white deposits that accumulate under the retina, typically between the retinal pigment epithelium and Bruch's membrane. They are a hallmark of early AMD.

Clinical Profile:Blurred vision, metamorphopsia (distortion of straight lines), central scotoma.

Risk Factors:Age (age-related macular degeneration), smoking, genetics.

Investigations:

Amsler Grid:To detect metamorphopsia or scotoma.

Fundus Fluorescein Angiography (FFA):To confirm leakage from CNVM, classify types (classic, occult), and identify feeder vessels.

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):Essential for visualizing subretinal fluid, intraretinal fluid, subretinal hemorrhage, and the CNVM itself. It also helps monitor response to treatment. Enhanced-depth imaging OCT can show choroidal thickening.

Management:

Anti-VEGF Injections:Intravitreal injections of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) agents (e.g., ranibizumab, aflibercept, bevacizumab) are the primary treatment for wet AMD with CNVM.

Photodynamic Therapy (PDT):Less commonly used now, but can be an option in specific cases.

Laser Photocoagulation:Used rarely for well-demarcated extrafoveal CNVM.

Counseling:Patients need to be educated on the chronic nature of the disease, the need for regular follow-up, and monitoring with Amsler grids at home.

4. Visual field reporting. Causes of inferior field defects.

Visual Field Reporting:Involves interpreting perimetry results (e.g., Humphrey Visual Field) to identify patterns of vision loss.

Preliminary Instructions:Explain the test to the patient, cover one eye, ask them to fixate on a central target, and report any parts of the test target that are unclear or missing.

Common Clinical Syndromes:Bitemporal hemianopia, homonymous hemianopia, bitemporal or homonymous quadrantanopia, altitudinal hemianopia.

Causes of Inferior Field Defects:

Glaucoma:Inferior arcuate scotoma or nasal step due to superior nerve fiber layer damage.

Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy (AION):Especially non-arteritic AION, can cause altitudinal visual field defects (often inferior).

Retinal Detachment (Superior):A superior retinal detachment would cause an inferior visual field defect.

Superior Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO):Can cause an inferior visual field defect.

Optic Nerve Coloboma:Can cause a variety of field defects, including inferior.

Compressive Lesions:Depending on location, can cause various defects.

Investigations:Full ophthalmic examination including optic disc assessment (for cupping, pallor, edema), intraocular pressure measurement, and imaging studies (OCT of RNFL, MRI/CT if neurological cause suspected).

5. FFA of peripheral neovascularisation. DD and management.(Diabetic retinopathy and sickle cell etc)

Explanation of FFA:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Fundus fluorescein angiography is a diagnostic procedure that uses a fluorescent dye injected intravenously to visualize the retinal and choroidal vasculature and detect abnormalities like leakage, non-perfusion, or neovascularization.

Explanation of Peripheral Neovascularisation:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". New, abnormal blood vessel growth in the peripheral retina, which is fragile and prone to bleeding.

Differential Diagnosis:

Diabetic Retinopathy (Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy - PDR):The most common cause, characterized by neovascularization elsewhere (NVE) or neovascularization of the disc (NVD).

Sickle Cell Retinopathy:Neovascularization often takes the form of "sea fan" neovascularization, associated with peripheral non-perfusion.

Eales Disease:An idiopathic inflammatory occlusive vasculitis primarily affecting the peripheral retinal veins, leading to ischemia and neovascularization [Outside Source, 671].

Sarcoidosis:Can cause retinal vasculitis and neovascularization.

Retinal Vein Occlusions (Branch or Central):Can lead to retinal ischemia and secondary neovascularization.

Retinopathy of Prematurity (ROP):In infants, can cause abnormal vessel growth in the peripheral retina.

Management:

Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP):The primary treatment to ablate ischemic peripheral retina and regress neovascularization.

Anti-VEGF Injections:Can be used as an adjunct to PRP, especially in cases of active bleeding or macular edema.

Vitrectomy:Indicated for non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment, or combined tractional-rhegmatogenous retinal detachment.

Systemic Control:Crucial to manage underlying systemic conditions like diabetes and hypertension.

6. Acute congestive glaucoma DD and detailed management. Causes and site of glaucoma fleken

Explanation of Acute Congestive Glaucoma:Not explicitly defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". This typically refers to acute primary angle closure glaucoma (PACG).

Differential Diagnosis:

Acute Primary Angle Closure Glaucoma (PACG):Most common cause. Characterized by sudden severe eye pain, headache, blurred vision, colored halos, red eye, steamy cornea, mid-dilated fixed pupil, and very high IOP. Pathogenesis involves relative pupil block, anterior iris-lens diaphragm, and narrow angles.

Neovascular Glaucoma:Secondary to retinal ischemia (e.g., PDR, CRVO), leading to neovascularization of the iris and angle.

Uveitic Glaucoma:Secondary to inflammation causing trabecular meshwork dysfunction or synechiae.

Phacomorphic Glaucoma:Angle closure due to a swollen cataractous lens pushing the iris forward.

Lens-Particle Glaucoma:Inflammation and angle blockage from retained lens material after trauma or surgery.

Post-Traumatic Glaucoma:Can be due to angle recession, hyphema, or inflammation.

Clinical Profile:As above for PACG: severe pain, blurred vision, halos, red eye, steamy cornea, mid-dilated pupil, very high IOP.

Investigations:

Gonioscopy:Essential to confirm angle closure.

Slit Lamp Examination:To assess corneal edema, anterior chamber depth, presence of flare/cells, iris changes, and glaukomflecken.

IOP Measurement:Crucially elevated.

Fundus Examination:To assess optic nerve head.

Management:

Acute Phase:

IOP Lowering:Topical beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors; systemic acetazolamide; hyperosmotic agents (glycerol, mannitol).

Miotics:Pilocarpine to constrict pupil and open the angle (after IOP reduction).

Anti-inflammatory:Topical corticosteroids.

Laser Peripheral Iridotomy (LPI):Definitive treatment to relieve pupil block and open the angle. Performed in the affected eye and often prophylactically in the contralateral eye.

Chronic Management:Monitor IOP, optic nerve, visual fields; consider trabeculectomy if LPI is insufficient or in cases of chronic angle closure.

Glaukomfleken:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". These are small, grayish-white subcapsular opacities in the anterior lens capsule, typically seen after an acute attack of angle-closure glaucoma.

Causes and Site of Glaukomfleken:Caused by ischemic necrosis of lens epithelial cells due to sudden, severe elevation of IOP during an acute angle-closure attack. Site is typically the anterior subcapsular region of the lens.

III. Ophthalmic Surgery

1. PXF and nucleus drop

Explanation of PXF:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Pseudoexfoliation syndrome is an age-related systemic disorder characterized by the production and deposition of an abnormal fibrillar extracellular material, primarily in the anterior segment of the eye, but also in other organs.

Problems with PXF in Cataract Surgery:

Weak Zonules:The most significant problem. Pseudoexfoliation material deposits on zonules, leading to zonulopathy, which increases the risk of zonular dialysis, capsular rupture, and nucleus drop during phacoemulsification.

Poor Pupil Dilation:Often a feature of PXF, making surgery more challenging.

Glaucoma:PXF is the most common cause of secondary open-angle glaucoma. Pre-existing high IOP needs to be managed.

Explanation of Nucleus Drop:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". This refers to the nucleus of the crystalline lens falling into the vitreous cavity during cataract surgery, usually due to extensive zonular or posterior capsular rupture.

Management:

Preoperative:Careful assessment of zonular integrity (phacodonesis, iris transillumination), pupil dilation, and IOP control. Counsel patient about increased risks.

Intraoperative:Use of capsular tension rings (CTRs) or segments for zonular support. Viscoelastics to protect endothelium and maintain space. Low phaco power and careful technique to minimize stress on zonules. May need conversion to ECCE or scleral fixation of IOL.

If Nucleus Drop Occurs:Stop phacoemulsification, close wounds, and refer to a vitreoretinal surgeon for pars plana vitrectomy and nucleus removal. Do not attempt to retrieve the nucleus from the vitreous in the anterior segment.

2. Refractive surprise

Explanation of Refractive Surprise:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". This refers to a postoperative refractive error that is significantly different from the intended refractive target after cataract or refractive surgery.

Causes:

Preoperative Factors:Inaccurate biometry (axial length measurement, corneal power), incorrect IOL power calculation formula, uncorrected astigmatism, previous corneal refractive surgery, ocular surface disease affecting keratometry.

Intraoperative Factors:Incorrect IOL placement (wrong orientation for toric IOL), IOL decentration or tilt, wound issues, intraocular lens power error from manufacturer.

Postoperative Factors:IOL shift, wound healing changes, corneal edema, macular edema (CMO), capsular bag distension syndrome.

Investigations:

Review Preoperative Data:Recheck biometry, IOL calculations, and records.

Ocular Examination:Thorough slit lamp exam for IOL position, corneal edema, ocular surface disease, wound integrity. Dilated exam for IOL alignment (toric IOLs) and posterior segment pathology (CMO).

OCT:Macular OCT for CME. AS-OCT for wound healing or Descemet's detachment.

Biometry and Topography:Repeat measurements.

Management:

Initial Assessment:Rule out secondary pathology. Discuss with the patient about their satisfaction and desire for further correction. Spectacles or contact lenses should always be offered.

Timing:Wait 2-3 months after initial surgery to allow wounds to stabilize and refraction to be stable.

Surgical Options:

IOL Exchange:If the refractive error is significant and due to an incorrect IOL power [Outside Source].

Piggyback IOL:Placing an additional IOL on top of the existing one [Outside Source].

Corneal Refractive Surgery:LASIK or PRK for residual astigmatism or spherical error.

Limbal Relaxing Incisions (LRIs) / Corneal Relaxing Incisions (CRIs):For astigmatism.

Prevention:Accurate biometry, appropriate IOL selection, and meticulous surgical technique. Protection of endothelium by dispersive viscoelastic.

3. Trachoma with entropion and surgeries

Explanation of Trachoma:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Trachoma is a chronic keratoconjunctivitis caused byChlamydia trachomatis, leading to scarring of the conjunctiva, trichiasis, and corneal opacification, often resulting in blindness.

Explanation of Entropion:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Entropion is an eyelid malposition where the eyelid margin turns inward, causing the eyelashes to rub against the cornea (trichiasis).

Causes of Entropion (in Trachoma):Cicatricial changes in the tarsal conjunctiva due to chronic inflammation and scarring in trachoma lead to inward rotation of the eyelid margin.

Clinical Profile:Foreign body sensation, tearing, redness, corneal irritation, trichiasis, corneal ulceration, scarring, and visual impairment.

Management (Surgical):

Lid Surgery:Various surgical techniques aim to correct the entropion and associated trichiasis. These often involve everting the tarsal plate (e.g., bilamellar tarsal rotation procedures like the bilamellar tarsal rotation (BTR) or posterior lamellar tarsal rotation (PLTR)).

Epilation/Cryotherapy:For isolated misdirected lashes [Outside Source].

Corneal Grafting:If severe corneal opacification has developed [Outside Source].

4. 4 yrs after trab comes with low iop causes and management

Explanation of Trab:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Trabeculectomy is a surgical procedure for glaucoma that creates a new drainage pathway for aqueous humor, forming a filtering bleb.

Causes of Low IOP 4 Years After Trabeculectomy:

Overfiltration/Excessive Drainage:Well-functioning bleb leading to chronically low IOP, sometimes associated with hypotony maculopathy.

Bleb Leak:A persistent leak from the filtering bleb, often identified with Seidel's test.

Cyclodialysis Cleft:Detachment of the ciliary body from the sclera, creating an alternative outflow pathway [Outside Source].

Ciliary Body Hypofunction:Decreased aqueous humor production [Outside Source].

Phthisis Bulbi:End-stage hypotony leading to a shrunken, non-functional eye.

Management:

Bleb Leak:Conservative (patching, cycloplegics, aqueous suppressants, bandage contact lens) or surgical repair (bleb revision, conjunctival flap advancement).

Overfiltration/Hypotony:May require bleb revision, scleral patch graft, or injection of autologous blood into the bleb to induce scarring and reduce filtration.

Phthisis Bulbi:Management is usually for pain and cosmesis, possibly evisceration or enucleation with prosthetic eye.

5. 2 weeks after trab shallow AC and high IOP

Causes of Shallow AC and High IOP 2 Weeks Post-Trabeculectomy:

Aqueous Misdirection (Malignant Glaucoma):Aqueous humor is misdirected into the vitreous cavity, pushing the lens-iris diaphragm forward, leading to shallow AC and often high IOP.

Pupillary Block:Incompetent peripheral iridotomy (PI) or posterior synechiae can cause pupil block, leading to iris bombé and shallow AC. This is less likely with high IOP unless total angle closure has occurred.

Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage:Accumulation of blood in the suprachoroidal space, causing anterior displacement of the iris-lens diaphragm and shallow AC. Often associated with pain and sudden vision loss.

Blockage of Drainage Pathway:Inflammatory debris or fibrinous material blocking the sclerostomy site, leading to bleb failure and high IOP [Outside Source].

Expulsive Hemorrhage:A rare, severe complication causing acute shallowing of the AC and high IOP, often with globe rupture [Outside Source].

Management:

Aqueous Misdirection:Medical management (cycloplegics, aqueous suppressants, hyperosmotic agents), YAG laser posterior capsulotomy/hyaloidotomy, or surgical vitrectomy.

Pupillary Block:Laser peripheral iridotomy if not patent or surgical iridectomy.

Suprachoroidal Hemorrhage:Close observation if small; surgical drainage if extensive, painful, or causing globe compromise.

Bleb Blockage:Intensive topical steroids, massage, or surgical bleb revision [Outside Source].

6. Corneal lattice dystrophy with management

Explanation of Corneal Lattice Dystrophy:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". It is an inherited stromal corneal dystrophy characterized by branching, refractile, lattice-like lines in the corneal stroma.

Inheritance:Autosomal dominant.

Clinical Profile:Progressive vision loss due to corneal opacification and recurrent corneal erosions.

Management:

Recurrent Corneal Erosions:Lubricating eye drops, therapeutic contact lenses, topical antibiotics, anterior stromal puncture, phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK).

Vision Loss due to Opacification:

Phototherapeutic Keratectomy (PTK):For superficial opacities [Outside Source].

Corneal Transplant (Penetrating Keratoplasty - PKP or Deep Anterior Lamellar Keratoplasty - DALK):For deeper, visually significant opacities.

Recurrence:Lattice dystrophy can recur in the corneal graft after PKP.

IV. Clinical Cases (from Candidate 198, Hyderabad 2016)

A. Anterior Segment:

1. Penetrating corneal transplant with clear graft with peaked pupil with PCIOL with PCO with iris pigment dispersion on graft

Explanation of Penetrating Corneal Transplant:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Full-thickness corneal replacement surgery (PKP).

Explanation of PCIOL:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Posterior Chamber Intraocular Lens, an artificial lens implanted behind the iris, typically during cataract surgery.

Explanation of PCO:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Posterior Capsular Opacification, a common late complication of cataract surgery where residual lens epithelial cells proliferate on the posterior capsule, causing clouding.

Explanation of Peaked Pupil:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". An irregularly shaped pupil, often peaked or drawn towards an area of iris adhesion or wound.

Explanation of Iris Pigment Dispersion on Graft:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.16". Pigment deposition on the corneal graft endothelium, possibly from irritation of the iris by the IOL or inflammation [Outside Source].

Clinical Profile:Good visual acuity if the graft is clear, but PCO would reduce vision. Peaked pupil could indicate iris incarceration in the wound or synechiae. Pigment dispersion suggests ongoing irritation or inflammation.

Causes:

Peaked Pupil:Iris incarceration in the graft wound, synechiae, or previous surgical manipulation.

PCO:Proliferation of lens epithelial cells after cataract surgery.

Pigment Dispersion:Friction between IOL and iris, or inflammation [Outside Source].

Management:

PCO:YAG laser posterior capsulotomy.

Peaked Pupil/Iris Incarceration:May require surgical revision of the iris or wound.

Pigment Dispersion:Monitor IOP; if pigmentary glaucoma develops, manage medically or surgically [Outside Source].

2. Stromal Corneal dystrophy probably granular

Explanation of Stromal Corneal Dystrophy:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". A group of inherited disorders affecting the corneal stroma, leading to deposition of abnormal material and progressive vision loss. Granular dystrophy is a type of stromal dystrophy [Outside Source].

Clinical Profile:Progressive vision loss due to corneal opacities. Granular dystrophy typically presents with discrete, grayish-white, breadcrumb-like opacities in the central stroma [Outside Source].

Management:

Phototherapeutic Keratectomy (PTK):For superficial opacities [Outside Source].

Corneal Transplant (PKP or DALK):For deeper, visually significant opacities. Recurrence can occur in the graft.

3. Trab with bleb

Explanation of Trab with Bleb:As explained before, trabeculectomy is glaucoma surgery creating a filtering bleb. A bleb is a subconjunctival fluid-filled sac that allows aqueous humor to filter out of the eye, lowering IOP.

Clinical Profile:The appearance of the bleb (size, height, vascularity, presence of leaks or infection) indicates its function and health. A healthy bleb is typically diffuse, avascular, and slightly elevated.

Complications:Blebitis (infection of the bleb), bleb leak, hypotony, fibrosis leading to bleb failure and high IOP, shallow anterior chamber.

Management:Varies greatly depending on the complication (e.g., antibiotics for blebitis, bleb revision for leaks or failure).

B. Oculoplasty

1. Proptosis with cork screw vessels with Carotid-cavernous fistula

Explanation of Proptosis:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Proptosis (or exophthalmos) is the anterior displacement of the globe.

Explanation of Cork Screw Vessels:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Dilated and tortuous conjunctival or episcleral vessels, appearing like corkscrews, are a classic sign of increased venous pressure, often seen in carotid-cavernous fistula.

Explanation of Carotid-Cavernous Fistula (CCF):Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". An abnormal connection between the carotid artery (or its branches) and the cavernous sinus, leading to high-pressure arterial blood flowing into the venous system.

Clinical Profile:

Ocular:Pulsating proptosis, orbital bruit (swishing sound heard with stethoscope over the eye/orbit), chemosis, conjunctival injection with "corkscrew" vessels, elevated IOP, ophthalmoplegia (restricted eye movements due to venous congestion of ocular muscles or cranial nerve palsies), vision loss (due to optic neuropathy or severe venous congestion).

Systemic:Headache, sometimes intracranial hemorrhage [Outside Source].

Causes:Trauma (most common, especially direct CCF), spontaneous (dural CCF, often in older women with atherosclerosis) [Outside Source].

Differential Diagnosis of Proptosis (Life-threatening conditions to rule out):Orbital cellulitis, orbital tumors (rhabdomyosarcoma, optic nerve glioma, meningioma, metastases), orbital inflammatory disease (pseudotumor), thyroid eye disease, cavernous sinus thrombosis, vascular lesions (varix).

Investigations:

Ocular:Visual acuity, pupillary exam, EOM, IOP. Auscultation for bruit.

Imaging:CT or MRI of orbits and brain, CTA/MRA for vascular anatomy. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) is gold standard for diagnosis and mapping.

Management:

Referral:Urgent referral to neuro-interventional radiologist or neurosurgeon.

Treatment:Endovascular embolization is the primary treatment, using coils or balloons to close the fistula [Outside Source]. Conservative management for some low-flow dural fistulas [Outside Source].

Complications of not referring:Can be fatal if not referred.

2. Proptosis with elevation and abduction absent (i.e. inferior rectus and medial rectus restriction-- Thyroid eye disease). However, the eye was in general very quiet and there was no redness at all.

Explanation of Thyroid Eye Disease (TED):Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". An autoimmune inflammatory disorder affecting the orbit, primarily the extraocular muscles and orbital fat, leading to proptosis, lid retraction, restrictive myopathy, and optic neuropathy.

Clinical Profile:

Ocular:Proptosis (can be unilateral or bilateral), lid retraction, lid lag, restrictive ophthalmopathy (most commonly inferior rectus, leading to limited upgaze, and medial rectus, leading to limited abduction), diplopia, exposure keratopathy, optic neuropathy. The patient describes (elevation and abduction absent) implies restriction of the inferior and medial rectus muscles. The absence of redness indicates the disease may be in a quiescent (inactive) phase.

Systemic:Associated with thyroid dysfunction (hyperthyroidism, euthyroid, or hypothyroidism).

Risk Factors:Smoking is a significant risk factor for worse TED.

Investigations:

Thyroid Function Tests:TSH, T3, T4, thyroid autoantibodies (TRAb, anti-TPO, anti-TG).

Imaging (CT/MRI orbits):To visualize enlarged extraocular muscles (typically sparing the tendons), increased orbital fat, and assess optic nerve compression.

Ocular:Visual acuity, color vision, pupillary examination, exophthalmometry, full ocular motility assessment.

Management:

Systemic Thyroid Control:Optimal management of thyroid function.

Active Disease (Inflammatory Phase):Systemic corticosteroids are the mainstay. Orbital radiotherapy may also be used.

Inactive Disease (Fibrotic Phase):Surgical management is typically performed in a staged approach:

Orbital Decompression:For severe proptosis, optic nerve compression, or exposure keratopathy.

Strabismus Surgery:To correct diplopia after orbital decompression.

Lid Surgery:To correct lid retraction and improve cosmesis/exposure.

General:Lubricants for dry eye, prisms for minor diplopia, smoking cessation counseling.

C. Posterior Segment

1. Right eye inferior branch retinal vein occlusion with vitritis/Vitreous hemorrhage with CME, left eye white subretinal patches near the fovea. DD BRVO or Vasculutis (Eales/Sarcoidosis etc)

Explanation of BRVO:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Branch retinal vein occlusion is blockage of a branch of the retinal vein, leading to hemorrhage, edema, and ischemia in the affected retinal sector.

Explanation of Vitritis/Vitreous Hemorrhage:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Vitritis is inflammation of the vitreous (vitreous cells and haze). Vitreous hemorrhage is bleeding into the vitreous cavity, causing sudden vision loss or floaters.

Explanation of CME:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Cystoid Macular Edema is fluid accumulation in the macula, forming cyst-like spaces, causing blurred vision.

Clinical Profile (BRVO):Sudden, painless vision loss or visual field defect. Fundus shows flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and macular edema in the affected sector.

Differential Diagnosis:

BRVO:The most direct cause of the described findings.

Vasculitis:

Eales Disease:Peripheral retinal vasculitis with recurrent vitreous hemorrhage, often bilateral, in young adults.

Sarcoidosis:Can cause retinal vasculitis (candle-wax dripping periphlebitis), vitritis, and vitreous hemorrhage.

Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE):Can cause retinal vasculitis, cotton wool spots, hemorrhages.

Other Collagen Vascular Diseases:(e.g., Polyarteritis Nodosa - PAN, Wegener's Granulomatosis).

White subretinal patches (Left eye):This points to a different pathology. Possibilities include multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS), acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR), multifocal choroiditis, presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome (POHS). These are typically inflammatory or infectious.

Systemic Risk Factors for BRVO:Hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, glaucoma.

Investigations:

Ocular:

FFA:To assess non-perfusion, leakage, and neovascularization in BRVO. For white dots, FFA may show punctate hyperfluorescence.

OCT:To quantify macular edema in BRVO and assess other retinal changes.

B-scan Ultrasound:If vitreous hemorrhage obscures view of the retina.

Systemic:Blood pressure, fasting blood glucose, lipid profile, CBC, ESR, CRP, syphilis serology, TB workup (Mantoux/IGRA), ANA, ANCA, specific tests for underlying systemic vasculitis if suspected.

Management (BRVO with CME/VH):

Macular Edema:Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections or corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone implant). Grid laser photocoagulation can be used for persistent macular edema due to non-ischemic BRVO.

Vitreous Hemorrhage:Observation, vitrectomy if non-clearing or associated with tractional retinal detachment.

Neovascularization:PRP if ischemic areas develop.

Systemic Management:Control systemic risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia).

Management (White Subretinal Patches):Depends on the specific diagnosis. Many white dot syndromes are self-limiting; corticosteroids or immunosuppressants may be used for inflammatory causes.

2. Retinal detachment with PVR with narrow funnel

Explanation of Retinal Detachment (RD):Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Separation of the neurosensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium.

Explanation of PVR:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Proliferative Vitreoretinopathy, a severe complication of RD characterized by the proliferation of cells on both sides of the retina and in the vitreous, leading to retinal traction, shortening, and fixed folds, often forming a "funnel" configuration.

Clinical Profile:Floaters, flashes of light (photopsia), visual field defect (curtain-like vision loss), decreased visual acuity. PVR indicates chronicity and more severe traction.

Causes of RD:

Rhegmatogenous RD:Most common, caused by a retinal break (tear or hole) allowing vitreous fluid to pass into the subretinal space.

Tractional RD:Caused by vitreoretinal traction, often due to proliferative diabetic retinopathy or retinopathy of prematurity.

Exudative/Serous RD:Caused by fluid leakage from the choroid or retina, without a break, often due to inflammatory conditions, tumors, or central serous chorioretinopathy.

Risk Factors:Myopia, previous cataract surgery, trauma, lattice degeneration, PVR.

Investigations:

Dilated Fundus Examination:Indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral depression is essential to visualize the retina, identify breaks, and assess PVR.

B-scan Ultrasound:If media opacities (e.g., dense cataract, vitreous hemorrhage) preclude direct visualization.

Management:

Surgical Repair:RD is primarily a surgical emergency.

Scleral Buckling:Involves placing a silicone band around the sclera to indent the eye wall, supporting retinal breaks and relieving vitreoretinal traction.

Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV):Surgical removal of the vitreous, internal drainage of subretinal fluid, relief of traction, and endolaser photocoagulation to seal breaks. Often combined with tamponade (silicone oil or gas). Essential for PVR.

Pneumatic Retinopexy:Gas injection into the vitreous combined with laser or cryopexy for selected RDs.

Tamponade:Silicone oil or expansile gases (e.g., C3F8) are used to provide internal tamponade against the retina after vitrectomy.

Counseling:Patients need to be informed about the prognosis, which can be guarded with PVR, and potential for multiple surgeries.

3. Diabetic retinopathy

Explanation of Diabetic Retinopathy:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". A microvascular complication of diabetes affecting the retina, leading to vision loss.

Clinical Profile:Can be asymptomatic in early stages. Symptoms include blurred vision, floaters, sudden vision loss (from vitreous hemorrhage or RD), visual field defects.

Classification:

Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR):Characterized by microaneurysms, dot and blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA), and venous beading. Can be mild, moderate, or severe.

Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR):Characterized by neovascularization of the disc (NVD) or elsewhere (NVE), vitreous hemorrhage, and tractional retinal detachment.

Diabetic Macular Edema (DME):Fluid accumulation in the macula, can occur at any stage and is a common cause of vision loss.

Risk Factors:Duration of diabetes, poor glycemic control (HbA1c), hypertension, hyperlipidemia, nephropathy.

Investigations:

Dilated Fundus Examination:Stereoscopic view to assess for NVD, NVE, macular edema, hemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots.

FFA:To identify areas of ischemia, microaneurysm leakage, and neovascularization.

OCT:To detect and quantify macular edema, assess vitreoretinal traction, and monitor treatment response.

B-scan Ultrasound:If vitreous hemorrhage obscures view.

Systemic:HbA1c, blood pressure, renal function tests (urea, creatinine, microalbuminuria).

Management:

Systemic Control:Strict glycemic control, blood pressure control (ACE inhibitors are good for nephropathy), and lipid management are fundamental.

Laser Photocoagulation:

Panretinal Photocoagulation (PRP):For PDR to regress neovascularization.

Focal/Grid Laser:For clinically significant macular edema without ischemia.

Anti-VEGF Injections:For diabetic macular edema (DME) or as an adjunct for PDR.

Vitrectomy:For non-clearing vitreous hemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment, or combined detachments.

D. Neuro and Squint

1. Esotropia with IO overaction asked to do Hirshberg cover uncover and prism bar test

Explanation of Esotropia:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Inward deviation of one or both eyes.

Explanation of IO Overaction:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Overaction of the inferior oblique muscle, leading to elevation and excyclotorsion of the eye in adduction.

Explanation of Hirschberg Test:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". A simple test to estimate the angle of deviation by observing the position of the corneal light reflex relative to the pupil center.

Explanation of Cover-Uncover Test:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Used to detect a phoria (latent deviation) or tropia (manifest deviation).

Explanation of Prism Bar Test:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Used to measure the angle of ocular deviation by neutralizing the deviation with prisms.

Clinical Profile:Inward deviation of the eye, possibly with head tilt or abnormal head posture to compensate. IO overaction causes the eye to elevate and extort when looking inwards.

Causes of Esotropia:Accommodative esotropia, infantile esotropia, sixth nerve palsy, sensory esotropia, convergence excess.

Investigations:Full ophthalmic and orthoptic examination, including visual acuity, refraction, ocular motility, and detailed cover tests.

Management:

Refractive Correction:For accommodative esotropia.

Patching:For amblyopia if present.

Strabismus Surgery:To correct the deviation and address muscle imbalances (e.g., weakening procedures for IO overaction, recession of medial rectus for esotropia).

2. 3rd nerve palsy with pupil sparing

Explanation of 3rd Nerve Palsy:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Paralysis of the oculomotor nerve, affecting eye movements (adduction, elevation, depression) and often causing ptosis and pupillary dilation.

Explanation of Pupil Sparing:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". In a 3rd nerve palsy, if the pupil is not involved (i.e., it is not dilated and reactive to light), it suggests that the lesion affecting the nerve is less likely to be compressive (e.g., aneurysm) and more likely to be ischemic. This is due to the anatomical arrangement of parasympathetic fibers (responsible for pupil constriction) on the periphery of the nerve, making them vulnerable to compression but relatively spared in ischemic lesions.

Clinical Profile:Ptosis (drooping eyelid), impaired adduction, elevation, and depression of the affected eye, leaving it "down and out." If pupil-sparing, the pupil size and reactivity are normal. Binocular diplopia.

Causes:

Ischemic (Microvascular) Causes:Most common cause of pupil-sparing 3rd nerve palsy, often associated with diabetes or hypertension.

Compressive Causes:Aneurysms (especially posterior communicating artery), tumors, inflammation, trauma. These typically involve the pupil due to compression of the superficial parasympathetic fibers.

Other:Inflammation, demyelination (rare).

Investigations:

Urgent Neuroimaging:If pupil-sparing, current guidelines suggest that in isolated complete pupil-sparing 3rd nerve palsy, imaging (MRI/MRA) may not be urgent if risk factors for ischemia are present and evolution is monitored. However, if there are any atypical features or the palsy progresses, immediate imaging is required to rule out compression (e.g., aneurysm).

Systemic Workup:Blood glucose, blood pressure, lipid profile for ischemic risk factors.

Management:

Treat Underlying Cause:Control diabetes, hypertension for ischemic causes.

Observation:If ischemic, many cases resolve spontaneously over weeks to months [Outside Source].

Address Diplopia:Patching, prisms, or strabismus surgery once stable.

3. Severe ptosis with restricted movement in all gazes- CPEO

Explanation of Ptosis:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Drooping of the upper eyelid.

Explanation of Restricted Movement in all Gazes:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Generalized ophthalmoplegia, affecting all extraocular muscles.

Explanation of CPEO:Not defined in "merged_2016experiences.txt". Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia. It is a mitochondrial disorder characterized by progressive paralysis of the extraocular muscles, leading to severe ptosis and ophthalmoplegia (restricted eye movements).

Clinical Profile:

Ocular:Bilateral, symmetric, slowly progressive ptosis (often severe, necessitating a chin-up head posture) and ophthalmoplegia (limited eye movements in all directions). Bell's phenomenon may be preserved or absent.

Systemic:Can be isolated or part of a syndromic presentation (e.g., Kearns-Sayre syndrome, which includes CPEO, pigmentary retinopathy, and cardiac conduction abnormalities).

Differential Diagnosis:Myasthenia Gravis (MG), botulism, mitochondrial myopathies, brainstem lesions. MG can cause fluctuating ptosis and ophthalmoplegia but typically responds to Tensilon test.

Investigations:

Ocular:Detailed ptosis examination (levator function, margin reflex distance). Ocular motility assessment.

Systemic:Genetic testing for mitochondrial DNA mutations, muscle biopsy (ragged-red fibers), EMG. Consider cardiac workup for Kearns-Sayre syndrome [Outside Source].

Management:
